1 Introduction

Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (AQFT) is one of two axiomatic programmes for QFT that emerged in the 1950s, in response to the problem of making QFT mathematically precise. While Wightman’s programme [SW00] maintains an emphasis on quantum fields, AQFT [Haa96, Ara99], developed initially by Haag, Kastler, Araki and others, takes the more radical step on focussing on local observables, with the idea that fields can emerge as natural ways of labelling some of the observables. Like Wightman theory, its primary focus is on setting out a precise mathematical framework into which all QFTs worthy of the name should fit. This permits one to separate the general study of the structure and properties of QFT from the problem of constructing (by whatever means) specific QFT models that obey the assumptions. The early development of AQFT is well-described in the monographs of Haag [Haa96] and Araki [Ara99]. Mathematically, it makes extensive use of operator algebra methods and indeed has contributed to the theory of von Neumann algebras in return. Relevant aspects of operator algebra theory, with links to the physical context, can be found in the monographs of Bratteli and Robinson [BR87, BR97]. AQFT also comprises a lot of machinery for treating specific QFT models, which have some advantages relative to other approaches to QFT. During the last 20 years it has also been adapted to provide rigorous constructions of perturbative QFT, and also of some low-dimensional models, and its overall viewpoint has been particularly useful in the theory of quantum fields in curved spacetimes. A recent edited collection [BDFY15] summarises these developments, and the two recent monographs [Rej16, Düt19] in particular describe the application to perturbation theory, while [HS18] concerns entanglement measures in QFT. An extensive survey covering some of the topics presented here in much greater depth can be found in [HM07].

The purpose of these lectures is to present an introduction to AQFT that emphasises some of its original motivations and de-mystifies some of its terminology (GNS representations, spectrum condition, Reeh–Schlieder, type III factors, split property, superselection sectors…). We also emphasise features of QFT that sharply distinguish it from quantum mechanics and which can be seen particularly clearly in the AQFT framework. Our treatment is necessarily limited and partial; the reader is referred to the literature mentioned for more detail and topics not covered here.

The idea of algebraic formulations of quantum theory, which we describe in Section 2, can be traced back to Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics, in which the algebraic relations between observables are the primary data. Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, by contrast, starts with spaces of wavefunctions, on which the observables of the theory act in specific ways.

As far as position and momentum go, and for systems of finitely many degrees of freedom, the distinction is rather inessential, because the Stone-von Neumann theorem guarantees that any (sufficiently regular11 1 To deal with the technical problems of using unbounded operators.) irreducible representation of the commutation relations is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation. However, the angular momentum operators provide a classic example in which inequivalent physical representations appear, and it is standard to study angular momentum as an algebraic representation problem. However, it was a surprise in the development of QFT that unitarily inequivalent representations have a role to play here, and indeed turn out to be ubiquitous. Section 3 is devoted to the van Hove model, one of the first examples in which this was understood. The van Hove model concerns a free scalar field with an external source, and is explicitly solvable. However, one can easily find situations in which a naive interaction picture approach fails to reproduce the correct solution – a failure that can be clearly ascribed to a failure of unitary equivalence between different representations of the canonical commutation relations (CCRs).

After these preliminaries, we set out the main assumptions of Algebraic Quantum Field Theory in Sec. 4. In fact there are many variants of AQFT and we give a liberal set of axioms that can be strengthened in various ways. We also describe how some standard QFT models can be formulated in terms of AQFT. Although we focus on free theories, it is important to emphasise that AQFT is intended as a framework for all quantum field theories worthy of the name, and successfully encompasses some nontrivial interacting models in low dimensions. AQFT distinguishes between two levels of structure: on the one hand, the algebraic relations among observables and on the other, their concrete realisation as Hilbert space operators. The link is provided by the GNS representation theorem (described in Sec. 2.3) once a suitable state has been given. For this reason we spend some time on states of the free scalar field, describing in particular the quasi-free states, which have representations on suitable Fock spaces. These include the standard vacuum state as well as thermal states.

The remaining parts of the notes concern general features of AQFT models, where the power of the technical framework begins to come through. Among other things, we prove the Reeh–Schlieder theorem and discuss some of its consequences in Section 5, before turning in Section 6 to the structure of the local von Neumann algebras in suitable representations and the remarkable result (which we describe, but do not prove) that they are all isomorphic to the unique hyperfinite factor of type III1. The distinction between one theory and another therefore lies in the way these algebras are situated, relative to one another, within the algebra of bounded operators on the Hilbert space of the theory. Finally, Sections 7 and 8 discuss the split property and the theory of superselection sectors. Like the theory in Section 6, these are deep and technical subjects and our aim here is to present the main ideas and some outline arguments, referring the dedicated reader to the literature. On the subject of literature: in this pedagogical introduction we have tended to give references to monographs rather than original papers, so the reference list is certainly not intended as a comprehensive survey of the field.

These notes represent a merger and expansion of lectures given by CJF at the AEI in Golm (October, 2018) and by KR at the Raman Research Institute, Bangalore (January, 2019). We are grateful to the students and organisers of the lecture series concerned. We are also grateful to the organisers of the conference Progress and Visions in Quantum Theory in View of Gravity (Leipzig, October 2018) for the opportunity to contribute to their proceedings.

2 Algebraic quantum mechanics

2.1 Postulates of quantum mechanics

The standard formalism of quantum theory starts with a complex Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, whose elements ϕ∈ℋ\phi\in\mathcal{H} are called state vectors. (For convenience some basic definitions concerning operators on Hilbert space are collected in Appendix A.) The key postulates of quantum mechanics say that:

  • •

    Pure states of a quantum system are described by rays in ℋ\mathcal{H}, i.e. [ψ]:={λ​ψ|λ∈ℂ}[\psi]:=\{\lambda\psi|\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\}. Mixed states are described by density matrices, i.e., positive trace-class operators ρ:ℋ→ℋ\rho:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}, with unit trace.

  • •

    Observables are described by self-adjoint operators AA on ℋ\mathcal{H}. However, the self-adjoint operators corresponding to observables may be a proper subset of the self-adjoint operators on ℋ\mathcal{H}; in particular, this occurs if the system is subject to superselection rules.

The probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics22 2 For simplicity, we restrict to sharp measurements, avoiding the introduction of positive operator valued measures. is based on the idea that one can associate to a self-adjoint operator AA and a normalised state vector ψ∈ℋ\psi\in\mathcal{H} a probability measure μψ,A\mu_{\psi,A}, so that the probability of the measurement outcome to be within a Borel subset Δ⊂ℝ\Delta\subset\mathbb{R} (for instance, an interval [a,b][a,b]) is given by

Prob⁡(A∈Δ,ψ)=∫Δμψ,A​(λ)=⟨ψ|PA​(Δ)​ψ⟩,\Prob(A\in\Delta;\psi)=\int_{\Delta}\mu_{\psi,A}(\lambda)=\langle\psi|P_{A}(\Delta)\psi\rangle\,,

where PA​(Δ)P_{A}(\Delta) is the spectral projection of the operator AA associated with Δ\Delta, and indeed Δ→PA​(Δ)\Delta\to P_{A}(\Delta) determines a projection-valued measure. The probability measure μψ,A\mu_{\psi,A} depends only on the ray [ψ][\psi] and has support contained within the spectrum of AA. The moments of this measure are given by

νn:=∫λn​μψ,A​(λ)=⟨ψ,An​ψ⟩;\nu_{n}:=\int\lambda^{n}\mu_{\psi,A}(\lambda)=\left<\psi,A^{n}\psi\right>\,;

conversely, the moments determine the measure uniquely subject to certain growth conditions. For example, the Hamburger moment theorem [Sim98] guarantees uniqueness provided that there are constants CC and DD such that

|νn|≤C​Dn​n!for all n∈ℕ0.|\nu_{n}|\leq CD^{n}n!\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$.} (1)

Note, however, that there are many examples in quantum mechanics in which the moments grow too fast for the unique reconstruction of a probability measure.

Example 1.

Consider the quantum particle confined to an interval (−a,a)(-a,a) subject to either Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions at the endpoints, with corresponding Hamiltonian operators HDH_{D} or HNH_{N} respectively. Measurements of the energy in a state ψ∈L2​(−a,a)\psi\in L^{2}(-a,a) supported away from the endpoints are distributed according to probability distributions μψ,HD\mu_{\psi,H_{D}} and μψ,HN\mu_{\psi,H_{N}}, which differ because the spectra of HDH_{D} and HNH_{N} differ. However, they share a common moment sequence because HDH_{D} and HNH_{N} agree on state vectors supported away from the endpoints.

One can combine effects from two physical states described by state vectors ψ1\psi_{1} and ψ2\psi_{2} by building their superposition, which, however depends on the choice of representative state vectors, since the ray corresponding to

ψ=α​ψ1+β​ψ2\psi=\alpha\psi_{1}+\beta\psi_{2}

typically depends on the choice of α\alpha and β\beta. However, sometimes the relative phase between the state vectors we are superposing cannot be observed. For example, this occurs if ψ1\psi_{1} is a state of integer angular momentum, while ψ2\psi_{2} is a half-integer angular momentum state. The physical reason for this is that a 2​π2\pi-rotation cannot be distinguished from no rotation at all. Of course there are self-adjoint operators on the Hilbert space that do sense the relative phase: the point is that these operators are not physical observables.

Let us give a brief argument for the existence of superselection sectors when the theory possesses a charge QQ, which is supposed to be conserved in any interactions available to measure it. For simplicity, we assume that QQ has discrete spectrum. Let ψ\psi be any eigenstate Q​ψ=q​ψQ\psi=q\psi and let PP be any projection corresponding to a zero-one measurement. After an ideal measurement of PP in state ψ\psi returning the value 11, the system is in state P​ψP\psi. But as charge is conserved, P​ψP\psi must be an eigenstate of QQ with eigenvalue qq, so

Q​P​ψ=q​P​ψ=P​Q​ψ.QP\psi=qP\psi=PQ\psi.

We deduce that [Q,P]​ψ=0[Q,P]\psi=0 and, as the Hilbert space is spanned by eigenstates of QQ, it follows that QQ and PP commute. Furthermore, QQ commutes with every self-adjoint operator representing a physical observable because any spectral projection of such an operator also corresponds to a physical observable.

Mathematically, the allowed physical observables are all block diagonal with respect to a decomposition of the Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} as

ℋ=⨁i∈Iℋi,\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathcal{H}_{i}\,,

where II is some index set and the subspaces ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i} are called superselection sectors, which would be the charge eigenspaces in our example above. The relative phases between state vectors belonging to different sectors cannot be observed. One of the main motivations behind AQFT was to understand how superselection sectors arise in QFT. We will see that the different superselection sectors correspond to unitarily inequivalent representations of the algebra of observables.

2.2 Algebraic approach

The main feature of the algebraic description of quantum theory is that the focus shifts from states to observables, and their algebraic relations. It is worth pausing briefly to consider the motivation for an algebraic description of observables – this is a long story if told in full (see [Emc72]), but one can explain the essential elements quite briefly.

The central issue is to provide an operational meaning for the linear combination and product of observables. Let us suppose that a given observable is measured by a certain instrument; for measurements conducted in each particular state, the numerical readout on the instrument is statistically distributed in a certain way, so the observable may be thought of as a mapping from states to random variables taking values in ℝ\mathbb{R}. Given two such observables, we can form a third, by taking a fixed linear combination of the random variables concerned, restricting to real-linear combinations in the first instance. So there is a clear justification for treating the set of observables as a real vector space. Similarly, we may apply a function to an observable by applying it to the random variables concerned; this may be regarded as repainting the scale on the measuring instruments. Given any two observables AA and BB it is now possible to form the observable

A∘B:=12​((A+B)2−A2−B2),A\circ B:=\frac{1}{2}\left((A+B)^{2}-A^{2}-B^{2}\right), (2)

simply by forming linear combinations and squares. This may be regarded as a symmetrised product of AA and BB. The remaining problem, which is naturally where the hard work lies, is to find appropriate additional conditions under which the vector space of observables can be identified with the self-adjoint elements of a ∗*-algebra, so that A∘B=A​B+B​AA\circ B=AB+BA. We refer the reader to [Emc72]; however, it is clear that observables naturally admit some algebraic structure beyond that of a vector space.

The main postulates of quantum theory, in its algebraic form, are now formulated as follows:

  1. 1.

    A physical system is described by a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, whose self-adjoint elements are interpreted as the observables. It is conventional though slightly imprecise to call 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} the algebra of observables. In many situations we impose the stricter condition that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be a unital C∗C^{*}-algebra.

  2. 2.

    States are identified with positive, normalized linear functionals ω:𝒜→ℂ\omega:{\mathcal{A}}\to\mathbb{C}, i.e. we require ω⁡(A∗​A)≥0\omega(A^{*}A)\geq 0 for all A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}} and ω⁡(𝟙)=1\omega(\mathds{1})=1 as well as ω\omega being linear. The state is mixed if it is a convex combination of distinct states (i.e., ω=λ​ω1+(1−λ)​ω2\omega=\lambda\omega_{1}+(1-\lambda)\omega_{2} with λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), ω1≠ω2\omega_{1}\neq\omega_{2}) and pure otherwise.

Some definitions are in order.

Definition 2.

A ∗*-algebra (also called an involutive complex algebra) 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is an algebra over ℂ\mathbb{C}, together with a map, ∗:𝒜→𝒜{}^{*}:{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{A}}, called an involution, with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    for all A,B∈𝒜A,B\in{\mathcal{A}}: (A+B)∗=A∗+B∗(A+B)^{*}=A^{*}+B^{*}, (A​B)∗=B∗​A∗(AB)^{*}=B^{*}A^{*},

  2. 2.

    for every λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} and every A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}: (λ​A)∗=λ¯​A∗(\lambda A)^{*}=\overline{\lambda}A^{*},

  3. 3.

    for all A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}: (A∗)∗=A(A^{*})^{*}=A.

The ∗*-algebra is unital if it has an element 𝟙{\mathbb{1}} which is a unit for the algebraic product (A​𝟙=𝟙​A=AA{\mathbb{1}}={\mathbb{1}}A=A for all A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}) and is therefore invariant under the involution. Unless explicitly indicated otherwise, a homomorphism α:𝒜1→𝒜2\alpha:{\mathcal{A}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{A}}_{2} between two ∗*-algebras will be understood to be an algebraic homomorphism that respects the involutions ((α​A)∗=α⁡(A∗)(\alpha A)^{*}=\alpha(A^{*})) and preserves units (α​𝟙𝒜1=𝟙𝒜2\alpha{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}={\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}).

The bounded operators ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} form a ∗*-algebra, with the adjoint as the involution, but there are other interesting examples.

Exercise 3.

(Technical – for those familiar with unbounded operators.) Given a dense subspace 𝒟{\mathscr{D}} of a Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, let ℒ⁡(𝒟,ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathscr{D}},{\mathcal{H}}) be the set of all (possibly unbounded) operators AA on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} defined on, and leaving invariant, 𝒟{\mathscr{D}}, (i.e., D⁡(A)=𝒟D(A)={\mathscr{D}}, A​𝒟⊂𝒟A{\mathscr{D}}\subset{\mathscr{D}}) and having an adjoint with 𝒟⊂D⁡(A∗){\mathscr{D}}\subset D(A^{*}). Then ℒ⁡(𝒟,ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathscr{D}},{\mathcal{H}}) may be identified with a subspace of the vector space of all linear maps from 𝒟{\mathscr{D}} to itself. Verify that ℒ⁡(𝒟,ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathscr{D}},{\mathcal{H}}) is an algebra with respect to composition of maps and that the map A↦A∗|𝒟A\mapsto A^{*}|_{\mathscr{D}} is an involution on ℒ⁡(𝒟,ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathscr{D}},{\mathcal{H}}), making it a ∗*-algebra. Show also that ℒ⁡(ℋ,ℋ)=ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{H}})={\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}). (Hint: Use the Hellinger–Toeplitz theorem [RS80, §III.5].)

The algebra of bounded operators also carries a norm that is compatible with the algebraic structure in various ways. In general we can make the following definitions:

Definition 4.

A normed algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is an algebra equipped with a norm ∥.∥\|.\| satisfying

‖A​B‖≤‖A‖​‖B‖.\|AB\|\leq\|A\|\|B\|\,.

If 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is unital, then it is a normed unital algebra if in addition ‖𝟙‖=1\|\mathds{1}\|=1. If 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is complete in the topology induced by ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| then 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a Banach algebra; if, additionally, 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a ∗*-algebra and ‖A∗‖=‖A‖\|A^{*}\|=\|A\|, then 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a Banach ∗*-algebra or B∗B^{*}-algebra.

A C∗C^{*}-algebra is a particular type of B∗B^{*}-algebra.

Definition 5.

A C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a B∗B^{*}-algebra whose norm has the C∗C^{*}-property:

‖A∗​A‖=‖A‖​‖A∗‖=‖A‖2,∀A∈𝒜.\|A^{*}A\|=\|A\|\|A^{*}\|=\|A\|^{2},\hskip 10.00002pt\forall A\in{\mathcal{A}}\,.

The bounded operators ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}), with the operator norm, provide an important example of a C∗C^{*}-algebra. A useful property of unital C∗C^{*}-algebras is that homomorphisms between them are automatically continuous [BR87, Prop. 2.3.1], with unit norm.

Turning to our second postulate, the role of the state in the algebraic approach is to assign expectation values: if A=A∗A=A^{*}, we interpret ω⁡(A)\omega(A) as the expected value of AA if measured in the state ω\omega. At first sight this definition seems far removed from the notion of a state in conventional formulations of quantum mechanics. Let us see that it is in fact a natural generalisation.

Suppose for simplicity (and to reduce notation) that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is an algebra of bounded operators acting on a Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, with the unit of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} coinciding with the unit operator on ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Then every unit vector ψ∈ℋ\psi\in{\mathcal{H}} induces a vector state on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} by the formula

ωψ​(A)=⟨ψ|A​ψ⟩,\omega_{\psi}(A)=\langle\psi|A\psi\rangle,

as is seen easily by computing ⟨ψ|𝟙​ψ⟩=1\langle\psi|{\mathbb{1}}\psi\rangle=1 and ⟨ψ|A∗​A​ψ⟩=‖A​ψ‖2≥0\langle\psi|A^{*}A\psi\rangle=\|A\psi\|^{2}\geq 0.

Exercise 6.

Show that every density matrix (a positive trace-class operator ρ\rho on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} with tr⁡ρ=1\tr\rho=1) induces a state on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} according to

ωρ​(A)=tr⁡ρ​AA∈𝒜.\omega_{\rho}(A)=\tr\rho A\hskip 20.00003ptA\in{\mathcal{A}}.

However it is important to realise that, in general, not all algebraic states on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} need arise from vectors or density matrices in a given Hilbert space representation. A further important point is that the definition of a state is purely mathematical in nature. It is not guaranteed that all states correspond to physically realisable situations, and indeed a major theme of the subject is to identify classes of states and representations that, by suitable criteria, may be regarded as physically acceptable.

Exercise 7.

By mimicking the standard arguments from quantum mechanics or linear algebra, show that every state ω\omega on a ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} induces a Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

|ω⁡(A∗​B)|2≤ω⁡(A∗​A)​ω​(B∗​B)|\omega(A^{*}B)|^{2}\leq\omega(A^{*}A)\omega(B^{*}B) (3)

for all A,B∈𝒜A,B\in{\mathcal{A}}. Show also that ω⁡(A∗)=ω⁡(A)¯\omega(A^{*})=\overline{\omega(A)}, for any A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}. (Hint: consider the linear combination 𝟙+α​A{\mathbb{1}}+\alpha A, for α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}.)

2.3 States and representations

The Hilbert space formulation of quantum mechanics is too useful to be abandoned entirely and the study of Hilbert space representations forms an important part of AQFT. Let us recall a few definitions.

Definition 8.

A representation of a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} consists of a triple (ℋ,𝒟,π)({\mathcal{H}},{\mathscr{D}},\pi), where ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a Hilbert space, 𝒟{\mathscr{D}} a dense subspace of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, and π\pi a map from 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} to operators on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} with the following properties:

  • •

    each π⁡(A)\pi(A) has domain D⁡(π⁡(A))=𝒟D(\pi(A))={\mathscr{D}} and range contained in 𝒟{\mathscr{D}},

  • •

    π⁡(𝟙)=𝟙|𝒟\pi({\mathbb{1}})={\mathbb{1}}|_{\mathscr{D}},

  • •

    π\pi respects linearity and products,

    π⁡(A+λ​B+C​D)=π⁡(A)+λ​π​(B)+π⁡(C)​π​(D),A,B,C,D∈𝒜,λ∈ℂ\pi(A+\lambda B+CD)=\pi(A)+\lambda\pi(B)+\pi(C)\pi(D),\hskip 20.00003ptA,B,C,D\in{\mathcal{A}},~\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
  • •

    each π⁡(A)\pi(A) has an adjoint with 𝒟⊂D⁡(π​(A)∗){\mathscr{D}}\subset D(\pi(A)^{*}), whose restriction to 𝒟{\mathscr{D}} obeys π​(A)∗|𝒟=π⁡(A∗)\pi(A)^{*}|_{\mathscr{D}}=\pi(A^{*}).

In short, π\pi is a homomorphism from 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} into the ∗*-algebra ℒ⁡(𝒟,ℋ)\mathcal{L}({\mathscr{D}},{\mathcal{H}}) defined in Exercise 3. Note that every π⁡(A)\pi(A) is closable, due to the fact that π​(A)∗\pi(A)^{*} is densely defined. We will also use the shorthand notation (ℋ,π)({\mathcal{H}},\pi) for a representation (ℋ,ℋ,π)({\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{H}},\pi). In this case, π\pi is a homomorphism π:𝒜→ℬ⁡(ℋ)\pi:{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}), and is necessarily continuous if 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a C∗C^{*}-algebra.

A representation π\pi is called faithful if ker⁡π={0}\ker\pi=\{0\}. It is called irreducible if there are no subspaces of ℋ\mathcal{H} invariant under π⁡(𝒜)\pi({\mathcal{A}}) that are not either trivial or dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Definition 9.

Two representations (ℋ1,𝒟1,π1)({\mathcal{H}}_{1},{\mathscr{D}}_{1},\pi_{1}) and (ℋ2,𝒟2,π2)({\mathcal{H}}_{2},{\mathscr{D}}_{2},\pi_{2}) of a ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} are called unitarily equivalent, if there is a unitary map U:ℋ1→ℋ2U:{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\rightarrow{\mathcal{H}}_{2} which restricts to an isomorphism between 𝒟1{\mathscr{D}}_{1} and 𝒟2{\mathscr{D}}_{2}, and U​π1​(A)=π2​(A)​UU\pi_{1}(A)=\pi_{2}(A)U holds for all A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}. They are unitarily inequivalent if they are not unitarily equivalent.

On a first encounter, algebraic states feel unfamiliar because one is so used to the Hilbert space version. However algebraic states are not too far away from a Hilbert space setting. The connection is made by the famous GNS (Gel’fand, Naimark, Segal) representation theorem.

Theorem 10.

Let ω\omega be a state on a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Then there is a representation (ℋω,𝒟ω,πω)({\mathcal{H}}_{\omega},{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega},\pi_{\omega}) of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and a unit vector Ωω∈𝒟ω\Omega_{\omega}\in{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} such that 𝒟ω=πω​(𝒜)​Ωω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}=\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}})\Omega_{\omega} and

ω⁡(A)=⟨Ωω|πω​(A)​Ωω⟩,∀A∈𝒜.\omega(A)=\langle\Omega_{\omega}|\pi_{\omega}(A)\Omega_{\omega}\rangle,\hskip 20.00003pt\forall~A\in{\mathcal{A}}. (4)

Furthermore (ℋω,𝒟ω,πω,Ωω)({\mathcal{H}}_{\omega},{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega},\pi_{\omega},\Omega_{\omega}) are unique up to unitary equivalence. If 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a C∗C^{*}-algebra, then, additionally, (i) each πω​(A)\pi_{\omega}(A) extends to a bounded operator on ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}; (ii) ω\omega is pure if and only if the representation is irreducible; and (iii) if πω\pi_{\omega} is faithful [i.e., πω​(A)=0\pi_{\omega}(A)=0 only if A=0A=0] then ‖πω​(A)‖=‖A‖𝒜\|\pi_{\omega}(A)\|=\|A\|_{{\mathcal{A}}}.

Due to the fact that πω​(𝒜)​Ωω\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}})\Omega_{\omega} is dense in ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}, we say that Ωω\Omega_{\omega} is cyclic for the representation. The existence of a link between purity and irreducibility is easily understood from the following example: if ψ,φ∈ℋ\psi,\varphi\in{\mathcal{H}} are linearly independent (normalised) vector states on a subalgebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}), then the density matrix state

ρ=λ⁡|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|+(1−λ)|φ⟩​⟨φ|0<λ<1\rho=\lambda|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|+(1-\lambda)|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|\hskip 20.00003pt0<\lambda<1

can be realised as the vector state Ψρ=λ​ψ⊕1−λ​φ\Psi_{\rho}=\sqrt{\lambda}\psi\oplus\sqrt{1-\lambda}\varphi in the reducible representation

A↦A⊕AA\mapsto A\oplus A

of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} on ℋ⊕ℋ{\mathcal{H}}\oplus{\mathcal{H}}.

Proof.

The construction of the GNS representation has several steps:

  • •

    Define a subset ℐω⊂𝒜{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}\subset{\mathcal{A}} by

    ℐω={A∈𝒜:ω⁡(A∗​A)=0}.{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}=\{A\in{\mathcal{A}}:\omega(A^{*}A)=0\}.

    Using the Cauchy–Schwarz identity (3), one may prove that ℐω{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega} is a left ideal: if A∈ℐωA\in{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega} then

    |ω⁡((B​A)∗​(B​A))|2=|ω⁡(C∗​A)|2≤ω⁡(C∗​C)​ω​(A∗​A)=0,|\omega((BA)^{*}(BA))|^{2}=|\omega(C^{*}A)|^{2}\leq\omega(C^{*}C)\omega(A^{*}A)=0,

    where C=B∗​B​AC=B^{*}BA, so B​A∈ℐωBA\in{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}. A similar argument shows that ℐω{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega} is a subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and that the subspace ℐω∗{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}^{*} is a right ideal. (Exercises!)

  • •

    Define a quotient vector space

    𝒟ω:=𝒜/ℐω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}:={\mathcal{A}}/{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}

    and note that 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} carries an inner product defined by

    ⟨[A]|[B]⟩=ω⁡(A∗​B)A,B∈𝒜,\langle[A]|[B]\rangle=\omega(A^{*}B)\hskip 20.00003ptA,B\in{\mathcal{A}},

    which is well-defined (i.e., independent of the choice of representatives, and has the properties of an inner product) due to the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and definition of ℐω{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega} (Exercises!). For example,

    ⟨[A]|[A]⟩=0⇔ω(A∗A)=0⇔A∈ℐω⇔[A]=0.\langle[A]|[A]\rangle=0\hskip 10.00002pt\iff\hskip 10.00002pt\omega(A^{*}A)=0\hskip 10.00002pt\iff\hskip 10.00002ptA\in{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}\hskip 10.00002pt\iff\hskip 10.00002pt[A]=0.
  • •

    Define the Hilbert space ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega} as the completion of 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} with respect to the inner product just mentioned; by construction 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} is dense in ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}.

  • •

    Define Ωω=[𝟙]∈𝒟ω⊂ℋω\Omega_{\omega}=[{\mathbb{1}}]\in{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}\subset{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}, noting that ‖Ωω‖2=ω⁡(𝟙)=1\|\Omega_{\omega}\|^{2}=\omega({\mathbb{1}})=1.

  • •

    Define πω\pi_{\omega} as follows: for each A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}, πω​(A)\pi_{\omega}(A) is the linear operator 𝒟ω→𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}\to{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} given by

    πω​(A)​[B]:=[A​B],B∈𝒜\pi_{\omega}(A)[B]:=[AB],\hskip 20.00003ptB\in{\mathcal{A}}

    which is well-defined due to the left-ideal property yet again. The properties

    πω​(𝟙)\displaystyle\pi_{\omega}({\mathbb{1}}) =𝟙ℋ\displaystyle={\mathbb{1}}_{\mathcal{H}}
    πω​(A+λ​B)\displaystyle\pi_{\omega}(A+\lambda B) =πω​(A)+λ​πω​(B)\displaystyle=\pi_{\omega}(A)+\lambda\pi_{\omega}(B)
    πω​(A​B)\displaystyle\pi_{\omega}(AB) =πω​(A)​πω​(B)\displaystyle=\pi_{\omega}(A)\pi_{\omega}(B)

    are easily verified as identities of operators on 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}, and it is clear that πω​(𝒜)​Ωω=𝒟ω\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}})\Omega_{\omega}={\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}, so Ωω\Omega_{\omega} is cyclic as 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} is dense.

    Now observe that

    ⟨πω​(A∗)​[B]|[C]⟩=⟨[A∗​B]|[C]⟩=ω⁡(B∗​A​C)=⟨[B]|πω​(A)​[C]⟩\langle\pi_{\omega}(A^{*})[B]|[C]\rangle=\langle[A^{*}B]|[C]\rangle=\omega(B^{*}AC)=\langle[B]|\pi_{\omega}(A)[C]\rangle

    for all [B],[C]∈𝒟ω[B],[C]\in{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}. This shows that πω​(A)\pi_{\omega}(A) has an adjoint with dense domain including 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} and indeed

    πω​(A∗)\displaystyle\pi_{\omega}(A^{*}) =πω​(A)∗|𝒟ω.\displaystyle=\pi_{\omega}(A)^{*}|_{{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}}.

    Therefore (ℋω,𝒟ω,πω)({\mathcal{H}}_{\omega},{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega},\pi_{\omega}) is a representation of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, and the calculation

    ⟨Ωω|πω​(A)​Ωω⟩=⟨[𝟙]|πω​(A)​[𝟙]⟩=⟨[𝟙]|[A]⟩=ω⁡(A)\langle\Omega_{\omega}|\pi_{\omega}(A)\Omega_{\omega}\rangle=\langle[{\mathbb{1}}]|\pi_{\omega}(A)[{\mathbb{1}}]\rangle=\langle[{\mathbb{1}}]|[A]\rangle=\omega(A)

    verifies (4).

  • •

    For uniqueness, suppose that another Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, dense domain 𝒟{\mathscr{D}}, distinguished vector Ω\Omega and representation π\pi are given with the properties stated above. Now define a linear map U:𝒟→𝒟ωU:{\mathscr{D}}\to{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} by

    U​π​(A)​Ω=πω​(A)​ΩωU\pi(A)\Omega=\pi_{\omega}(A)\Omega_{\omega}

    noting that this is well-defined because

    π⁡(A)​Ω=0⟹0=‖π⁡(A)​Ω‖ℋ2=ω⁡(A∗​A)=‖πω​(A)​Ωω‖ℋω2⟹πω​(A)​Ωω=0.\pi(A)\Omega=0\hskip 10.00002pt\implies\hskip 10.00002pt0=\|\pi(A)\Omega\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\omega(A^{*}A)=\|\pi_{\omega}(A)\Omega_{\omega}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}}^{2}\hskip 10.00002pt\implies\hskip 10.00002pt\pi_{\omega}(A)\Omega_{\omega}=0.

    Essentially the same calculation shows that UU is an isometry, and as it is clearly invertible, UU therefore extends to a unitary U:ℋ→ℋωU:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega} so that U​𝒟=𝒟ωU{\mathscr{D}}={\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}, U​Ω=ΩωU\Omega=\Omega_{\omega} and

    U​π​(A)​U−1=πω​(A)U\pi(A)U^{-1}=\pi_{\omega}(A)

    acting on any vector in 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega}. This is the promised unitary equivalence.

  • •

    The special features of C∗C^{*}-algebras are addressed e.g., in [BR87, Prop. 2.3.3 and §2.3.3] .

∎

Exercise 11.

Work through all the details in the proof of the GNS representation theorem.

3 Case study: the van Hove model

Our aim in this section is to present a version of van Hove’s model, one of the first instances in which it became clear that unitarily inequivalent representations of the CCRs arise naturally in QFT. van Hove’s work provided part of the motivation for Haag’s theorem on the nonexistence of the interaction picture and the subsequent development of AQFT.

The van Hove model [VH52] describes the interaction of a neutral scalar field with an external source; physically, it is a slightly simplified version of Yukawa’s model [Yuk35] of the mediation of internucleon forces by pions, and correctly accounts for the Yukawa interaction. The Lagrangian is

ℒ=12​(∇μϕ)​∇μϕ−12​m2​ϕ2−ρ​ϕ\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}(\nabla_{\mu}\phi)\nabla^{\mu}\phi-\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}-\rho\phi

using the +−−−{+}{-}{-}{-} signature conventions,33 3 We also adopt units in which the speed of light and ℏ\hbar are both set to 11. where the source ρ=ρ⁡(𝒙)\rho=\rho({\boldsymbol{x}}) is a time-independent real-valued function, or even a distribution: a simple nucleon model might have ρ\rho as a linear combination of δ\delta-functions.44 4 The Compton wavelength of the pions is approximately seven times that of a proton. The field equation is

(□+m2)​ϕ=−ρ.(\Box+m^{2})\phi=-\rho. (5)

Of course, ρ=0\rho=0 is the familiar massive real scalar field, and in general we know how to solve an inhomogeneous equation by finding a particular integral and reducing to a homogeneous equation. So this model ought to be (and is) exactly solvable. However, let us forget this for a moment and proceed according to standard lore (and in the first instance, a little formally), so as to exhibit the limitations of naive QFT.

We shall outline three quantization approaches. The first two follow the spirit of wave mechanics. Namely, having established a Hilbert space representation for the free field, we stick with it.

Method 1: Schrödinger picture

We work in the standard Fock space of the ρ=0\rho=0 model, in which there are ‘time zero’ fields φ⁡(𝒙)\varphi({\boldsymbol{x}}), π⁡(𝒙)\pi({\boldsymbol{x}}) obeying the equal time commutation relations

[φ⁡(𝒙),π⁡(𝒚)]=i​δ​(𝒙−𝒚)​𝟙.[\varphi({\boldsymbol{x}}),\pi({\boldsymbol{y}})]=i\delta({\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}})\mathbb{1}. (6)

To treat the ‘interacting’ model, one constructs its Hamiltonian HρH_{\rho} in terms of the canonical variables φ⁡(𝒙)\varphi({\boldsymbol{x}}), π⁡(𝒙)\pi({\boldsymbol{x}}), obtaining the Schrödinger picture evolution e−i​Hρ​te^{-iH_{\rho}t} of states. If desired, one can then pass to the interacting field in the Heisenberg picture as

Φρ​(t,𝒙)=ei​Hρ​t​φ​(𝒙)​e−i​Hρ​t.\Phi_{\rho}(t,{\boldsymbol{x}})=e^{iH_{\rho}t}\varphi({\boldsymbol{x}})e^{-iH_{\rho}t}.

Method 2: Interaction picture

In the interaction picture, the time-dependent field is given by the free field Φ0​(t,𝒙)\Phi_{0}(t,{\boldsymbol{x}}) acting on the usual Fock space. The interaction picture state evolution may be obtained e.g., using a perturbative Dyson expansion.

Methods 1 and 2 work perfectly well if ρ\rho is a smooth compactly supported function. However, one encounters problems if ρ\rho has δ\delta-singularities (for UV reasons) or if either m=0m=0 or ρ≡1\rho\equiv 1 (for IR reasons). The third method does not suffer these problems. It is more algebraic in nature and does not start from a prejudice about what the Hilbert space of the theory should be. Rather than treating the van Hove model as a modification of the free field, we quantize it directly.

Method 3: Canonical quantization from scratch

Start again with classical canonical variables φρ\varphi_{\rho} and πρ\pi_{\rho}. Making a Fourier analysis we may (without loss) write them in the form

φρ​(𝒙)\displaystyle\varphi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}}) =∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​12​ω​(a⁡(𝒌)+a​(−𝒌)∗)​ei​𝒌⋅𝒙\displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega}}(a({\boldsymbol{k}})+a(-{\boldsymbol{k}})^{*})e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}}
πρ​(𝒙)\displaystyle\pi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}}) =−i∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3ω2(a(𝒌)−a(−𝒌)∗)ei​𝒌⋅𝒙\displaystyle=-i\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2}}(a({\boldsymbol{k}})-a(-{\boldsymbol{k}})^{*})e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}}

for complex coefficients a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}}); here, the free mode frequency ω=‖𝒌‖2+m2\omega=\sqrt{\|{\boldsymbol{k}}\|^{2}+m^{2}} has been inserted for later convenience. Now promote the a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}})’s to ‘operators’ and impose the equal time commutation relations (6), whereupon the a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}}) must obey the CCRs

[a⁡(𝒌),a​(𝒌′)∗]=(2​π)3​δ​(𝒌−𝒌′)​𝟙[a({\boldsymbol{k}}),a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime})^{*}]=(2\pi)^{3}\delta({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime})\mathbb{1} (7)

and other commutators vanishing. Note that this is an entirely algebraic procedure and that nothing has yet been said about any Hilbert space representation. So the term ‘operator’ is a bit misleading as there is, as yet, nothing to operate on.

The next step is to introduce the Hamiltonian, which differs from the free Hamiltonian by the addition of the ρ​ϕ\rho\phi terms. Written in normal order, it is

Hρ=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​(ω​a​(𝒌)∗​a​(𝒌)+12​ω​(ρ^​(𝒌)¯​a​(𝒌)+ρ^​(𝒌)​a​(𝒌)∗)),H_{\rho}=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\left(\omega a({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}a({\boldsymbol{k}})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega}}\left(\overline{\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})}a({\boldsymbol{k}})+\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})a({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}\right)\right), (8)

where

ρ^(𝒌)=∫d3𝒙ρ(𝒙)e−i𝒌⋅𝒙\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\int d^{3}{\boldsymbol{x}}\,\rho({\boldsymbol{x}})e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}} (9)

is the Fourier transform of ρ\rho.

We now need to find a Hilbert space representation in which (give or take a constant) HρH_{\rho} is self-adjoint and the CCRs (7) are valid, and ideally we would like to find a vacuum state for HρH_{\rho}. This can be accomplished easily, by completing the square in (8) to give

Hρ=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​ω​a~​(𝒌)∗​a~​(𝒌)+Eρ​𝟙,H_{\rho}=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\omega\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})+E_{\rho}\mathbb{1}, (10)

where

a~​(𝒌)=a​(𝒌)+ρ^​(𝒌)2​ω3​𝟙,\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})=a({\boldsymbol{k}})+\frac{\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})}{\sqrt{2\omega^{3}}}\mathbb{1}, (11)

and the constant EρE_{\rho} is

Eρ=−∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3|ρ^​(𝒌)|22​ω2=12∫d3𝒙d3𝒚ρ(𝒙)VY(𝒙−𝒚)ρ(𝒚),E_{\rho}=-\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{|\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})|^{2}}{2\omega^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{3}{\boldsymbol{x}}\,d^{3}{\boldsymbol{y}}\,\rho({\boldsymbol{x}})V_{Y}({\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}})\rho({\boldsymbol{y}})\,, (12)

in which

VY​(𝒙)=−e−m​‖𝒙‖4​π​‖𝒙‖2V_{Y}({\boldsymbol{x}})=-\frac{e^{-m\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\|}}{4\pi\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^{2}}

is the Yukawa potential, responsible for the inter-nucleon force in this model. An important point is that the a~​(𝒌)\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}}) operators clearly obey the same CCRs as the a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}}).

It is now clear how to proceed: we should represent the a~​(𝒌)\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})’s and a~​(𝒌)∗\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}’s as Fock space annihilation and creation operators, writing Ω~\tilde{\Omega} for the ‘vacuum vector’ annihilated by the a~​(𝒌)\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})’s. Then Ω~\tilde{\Omega} is automatically a state of lowest energy for HρH_{\rho} and, by discarding the constant, we may arrange that it is a state of zero energy. Of course, the Fock space is just the usual bosonic Fock space over a 11-particle space L2​(ℝ3,d3​𝒌)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}) with Ω~\tilde{\Omega} as the vacuum vector, and our Hamiltonian is just the standard Hamiltonian of the free field on this space,

H~0=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​ω​a~​(𝒌)∗​a~​(𝒌).\tilde{H}_{0}=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\omega\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}}).

It may seem that this simply reproduces the situation of methods 1 or 2. However, the redefinition (11) provides the crucial difference, because the time-zero fields here are defined in terms of the original operators a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}}). Indeed, a calculation shows that the time-dependent Heisenberg picture field is

Φ~ρ​(t,𝒙)=ei​H~0​t​φρ​(𝒙)​e−i​H~0​t=Φ~0​(t,𝒙)+ϕρ​(𝒙)​𝟙,\tilde{\Phi}_{\rho}(t,{\boldsymbol{x}})=e^{i\tilde{H}_{0}t}\varphi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})e^{-i\tilde{H}_{0}t}=\tilde{\Phi}_{0}(t,{\boldsymbol{x}})+\phi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})\mathbb{1}, (13)

where

ϕρ(𝒙)=−∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3ρ^​(𝒌)ω2ei​𝒌⋅𝒙=−(VY⋆ρ)(𝒙)\phi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})=-\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})}{\omega^{2}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}}=-(V_{Y}\star\rho)({\boldsymbol{x}}) (14)

is (formally) a time-independent solution to the field equation (5), and

Φ~0​(t,𝒙)=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​12​ω​(a~​(𝒌)​e−i​ω​t+i​𝒌⋅𝒙+a~​(𝒌)∗​ei​ω​t−i​𝒌⋅𝒙)\tilde{\Phi}_{0}(t,{\boldsymbol{x}})=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega}}(\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})e^{-i\omega t+i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}}+\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}e^{i\omega t-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}}) (15)

is the standard free real scalar field on the Fock space.

On reflection, we see that the canonical quantization procedure amounts precisely to solving the inhomogeneous equation using a particular integral and a solution to the homogeneous equation, which we then quantize as a free scalar field with Ω~\tilde{\Omega} as its vacuum vector.

Provided that ϕρ\phi_{\rho} is at least a weak solution to (5), the final quantized model will be well-defined, in the sense that the fields give operator-valued distributions weakly solving the field equations and obeying the covariant commutation relations [which are actually the same as for the free field, as can be verified easily using Peierls method]. In particular, for m>0m>0, ρ\rho could be any tempered distribution, so linear combinations of δ\delta-functions, or ρ≡1\rho\equiv 1 are certainly permitted.

We can now discuss the relation of this model to the approach in Method 1, which started from the assumption that the time-zero fields of the van Hove model are exactly those of the free field. Our construction has actually shown that

φρ​(𝒙)=φ0​(𝒙)+ϕρ​(𝒙)​𝟙,πρ​(𝒙)=π0​(𝒙)\varphi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})=\varphi_{0}({\boldsymbol{x}})+\phi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})\mathbb{1},\hskip 20.00003pt\pi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})=\pi_{0}({\boldsymbol{x}}) (16)

where φ0\varphi_{0} and π0\pi_{0} are standard free-field time-zero fields in the vacuum representation. So methods 1 and 3 are equivalent if and only if there is a unitary map UU on the free field Fock space so that φρ​(𝒙)=U​φ0​(𝒙)​U−1\varphi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})=U\varphi_{0}({\boldsymbol{x}})U^{-1}, πρ​(𝒙)=U​π0​(𝒙)​U−1\pi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{x}})=U\pi_{0}({\boldsymbol{x}})U^{-1}, or equivalently, a⁡(𝒌)=U​a~​(𝒌)​U−1a({\boldsymbol{k}})=U\tilde{a}({\boldsymbol{k}})U^{-1}.

As the following exercise shows, a necessary (and in fact sufficient) condition for the existence of UU is that

∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​|ρ^​(𝒌)|22​ω3<∞,\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{|\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})|^{2}}{2\omega^{3}}<\infty, (17)

which fails for both δ\delta-function singularities and the limit ρ→1\rho\to 1. Whenever the integral in (17) diverges, method 1, and similarly method 2, therefore fail to reproduce the exact solution to the van Hove model.

Exercise 12.

Supposing that UU exists, deduce that ψ=U​Ω~\psi=U\tilde{\Omega} is annihilated by all a⁡(𝐤)a({\boldsymbol{k}}). Show that the nn-particle wavefunction component of ψ\psi is

ψn=1n​χρ⊗sψn−1,χρ​(𝒌)=ρ^​(𝒌)2​ω3,\psi_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\chi_{\rho}\otimes_{s}\psi_{n-1},\hskip 20.00003pt\chi_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\frac{\hat{\rho}({\boldsymbol{k}})}{\sqrt{2\omega^{3}}},

which implies that ψ=0\psi=0 unless χρ∈L2​(ℝ3,d3​𝐤/(2​π)3)\chi_{\rho}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}/(2\pi)^{3}), i.e., only if (17) holds. If it does hold, show further that

ψ=𝒩​∑n=0∞χρ⊗nn!\psi=\mathcal{N}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\chi_{\rho}^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}}

for some nonzero constant 𝒩∈ℂ\mathcal{N}\in\mathbb{C}, and hence ‖ψ‖=|𝒩|​e‖χρ‖2/2\|\psi\|=|\mathcal{N}|e^{\|\chi_{\rho}\|^{2}/2}.

The lessons to be drawn from the van Hove model are:

  • •

    Unitarily inequivalent representations of the CCRs appear naturally in QFT, even in simple models. In fact, were we to replace ρ↦λ​ρ\rho\mapsto\lambda\rho, we would find that the corresponding CCR representations are unitarily inequivalent for any distinct values of λ\lambda, when the integral in (17) diverges.

  • •

    The interaction picture does not exist in general. Haag’s theorem, a general result proved partly in response to the difficulties pointed out by van Hove, shows that the interaction picture is of very limited applicability: any QFT on Minkowski space whose time-zero fields coincide with those of a free field theory is necessarily a free field theory. It is sometimes said that Haag’s theorem applies only to translationally invariant theories; this is true of the formal statement, but the van Hove model with δ\delta-function potentials shows that the interaction picture can fail in nontranslationally invariant situations as well, or even in a finite volume box as in van Hove’s original paper.

  • •

    The success of Method 3 may be attributed to the way it separates the problem of determining the algebraic relations, treated first, from the problem of finding a Hilbert space representation, treated second.

4 Algebraic QFT

The appearance of unitarily inequivalent representations of the CCRs even in simple QFT models motivates an approach based in the first instance on algebraic relations. In this section we set out some minimal axioms for AQFT and then give constructions of some simple free QFTs in the AQFT framework and describe the class of quasifree states for the free scalar field.

4.1 Basic requirements

The minimum requirements (more or less) of AQFT on Minkowski spacetime 𝕄\mathbb{M} are:

  1. A1

    Local algebras
    There is a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) and, to each open causally convex55 5 A subset is causally convex if it contains every causal curve whose endpoints belong to it; see Fig. 1 for an illustration. bounded region 𝒪⊂𝕄\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{M}, a subalgebra 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) containing the unit of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}), so that the 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) collectively generate 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). We call 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) the quasi-local algebra of the theory.

  2. A2

    Isotony66 6 Doubtless to avoid ‘monotony’.
    Whenever 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}, the corresponding local algebras are nested,

    𝒜⁡(𝒪1)⊂𝒜⁡(𝒪2).{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\subset{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}). (18)
  3. A3

    Einstein causality
    If 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} are causally disjoint then

    [𝒜⁡(𝒪1),𝒜⁡(𝒪2)]=0,[{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}),{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})]=0, (19)

    i.e.,

    [A1,A2]=0,for all Ai∈𝒜⁡(𝒪i), i=1,2.[A_{1},A_{2}]=0,\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for all $A_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{i})$, $i=1,2$}. (20)
  4. A4

    Poincaré covariance
    To every transformation ρ\rho in the identity connected component 𝒫0{\mathcal{P}}_{0} of the Poincaré group, there is an automorphism α⁡(ρ)\alpha(\rho) of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) such that

    α⁡(ρ):𝒜⁡(𝒪)→𝒜⁡(ρ​𝒪)\alpha(\rho):{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})\to{\mathcal{A}}(\rho\mathcal{O}) (21)

    such that α⁡(id)=id𝒜⁡(𝕄)\alpha({\textrm{id}})={\textrm{id}}_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})} and naturally α⁡(σ)∘α⁡(ρ)=α⁡(σ∘ρ)\alpha(\sigma)\circ\alpha(\rho)=\alpha(\sigma\circ\rho) is required for any σ,ρ∈𝒫0\sigma,\rho\in{\mathcal{P}}_{0}.

  5. A5

    Existence of dynamics
    If 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2} and 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} contains a Cauchy surface of 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2},77 7 Recall that a Cauchy surface for 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} is a subset met exactly once by every inextendible timelike curve in 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. then

    𝒜⁡(𝒪2)=𝒜⁡(𝒪1).{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})={\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}). (22)

    Sometimes this condition is weakened.

The interpretation of this structure is that the self-adjoint elements of 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}), i.e., A=A∗∈𝒜⁡(𝒪)A=A^{*}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) are observables that are associated with the region 𝒪\mathcal{O}. Loosely, we may think of them as being measureable within 𝒪\mathcal{O}; this can be made more precise, see [FV18] and the short account [Few19]. We will use the term local observable algebra to describe 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}). The set of open causally convex bounded regions is a directed system under inclusion: given any two regions 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}, there exists a further region 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3} containing them both. For this reason the assignment 𝒪↦𝒜⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{O}\mapsto{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) is often called a net of local algebras. In this situation, the condition that the 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) collectively generate 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) reduces to the issue of whether 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) is equal to the union ⋃𝒪n𝒜⁡(𝒪n)\bigcup_{\mathcal{O}_{n}}{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{n}) [or its closure, if the algebras carry suitable topologies; see below], where 𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n} is any nested family of regions with ⋃n𝒪n=𝕄\bigcup_{n}\mathcal{O}_{n}=\mathbb{M}.

We will add more conditions in due course.

Remarks

  • •

    The prototypical local region is a double cone: namely, the set of all points lying on smooth timelike curves between two points pp and qq (with pp and qq excluded). By scalings, boosts and translations, all double cones in Minkowski space can be obtained from the elementary example

    𝒪={(t,𝒙)∈ℝ4:|t|+‖𝒙‖<ℓ0}\mathcal{O}=\{(t,{\boldsymbol{x}})\in\mathbb{R}^{4}:|t|+\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\|<\ell_{0}\}

    for some length-scale ℓ0>0\ell_{0}>0; see Fig. 1. All double cones are causally convex.

  • •

    For technical reasons it is often useful to require that each 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) is in fact a C∗C^{*}-algebra, but we need not insist on this, nor even that the 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) carry any topology. In the C∗C^{*}-case, one would require 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) to be generated in a C∗C^{*}-sense by the local algebras – technically it is their C∗C^{*}-inductive limit. In particular, the union ⋃𝒪𝒜⁡(𝒪)\bigcup_{\mathcal{O}}{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) would be dense in 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}).

  • •

    Sometimes (particularly in curved spacetimes) it is convenient to allow for local algebras indexed by unbounded (== noncompact closure) regions.

  • •

    Einstein causality requires elements of algebras of spacelike separated regions to commute. Therefore Fermi fields can only appear in products involving even numbers of fields. We return to this later.

  • •

    As mentioned, these are minimal requirements for AQFT but do not, by themselves, suffice to distinguish a quantum field theory from other relativistic models.

  • •

    Nothing has yet been said about Hilbert spaces, or about what algebraic states on the observable algebras are to be regarded as physical; we will discuss these issues later. Note that one can do quite a lot without ever going into Hilbert spaces. For example, let 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) be the algebra of the free real scalar field [see below], and let ω\omega be a state on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). Then the smeared nn-point function is

    Wn(f1,f2,…,fn):=ω(Φ(f1)Φ(f2)⋯Φ(fn)),f1,…,fn∈C0∞(𝕄)W_{n}(f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{n}):=\omega(\Phi(f_{1})\Phi(f_{2})\cdots\Phi(f_{n})),\hskip 20.00003ptf_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})

    and if this is suitably continuous w.r.t. the fif_{i}, it defines a distribution Wn∈𝒟′​(𝕄n)W_{n}\in{\mathscr{D}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{n}). Here, Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) denotes a ‘smeared field’ as will be described shortly. Therefore sufficiently regular states ω\omega define a hierarchy of distributional nn-point functions, without ever using a Hilbert space. Here, as elsewhere in these notes, C0∞​(𝕄)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}) denotes the space of smooth, complex-valued functions on 𝕄\mathbb{M} with compact support (i.e., vanishing outside a bounded set).

4.2 Examples

We continue by giving some specific examples of field theories in the framework of AQFT, drawing out various lessons as we go.

Free real scalar field

Consider the field equation

(□+m2)​ϕ=0(\Box+m^{2})\phi=0 (23)

and let E+E^{+} and E−E^{-} be the corresponding retarded and advanced Green operators, i.e., ϕ=E±​f\phi=E^{\pm}f solves the inhomogeneous equation

(□+m2)​ϕ=f(\Box+m^{2})\phi=f (24)

and the support of ϕ\phi is contained in the causal future (++, retarded) or causal past (−-, advanced) of the support of ff. Also define the advanced-minus-retarded solution operator E=E−−E+E=E^{-}-E^{+} and write

E⁡(f,g)=∫𝕄f⁡(x)​(E​g)​(x)​dvol𝕄​(x),E(f,g)=\int_{\mathbb{M}}f(x)(Eg)(x)\,{\textrm{dvol}}_{\mathbb{M}}(x)\,, (25)

where dvol𝕄​(x)≡d4​x{\textrm{dvol}}_{\mathbb{M}}(x)\equiv d^{4}x. The integral kernel is familiar from standard QFT:

E(x,y)=−∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3sin⁡k⋅(x−y)ω,E(x,y)=-\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\sin k\cdot(x-y)}{\omega}, (26)

where k∙=(ω,𝒌)k^{\bullet}=(\omega,{\boldsymbol{k}}), ω=‖𝒌‖2+m2\omega=\sqrt{\|{\boldsymbol{k}}\|^{2}+m^{2}}, and we use standard inertial coordinates on Minkowski spacetime.

Exercise 13.

Show that E⁡(x,y)|y0=x0=0E(x,y)|_{y^{0}=x^{0}}=0, and ∂y0E⁡(x,y)|y0=x0=δ⁡(𝐱−𝐲)\partial_{y^{0}}E(x,y)|_{y^{0}=x^{0}}=\delta({\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}}).

To formulate the quantized field in AQFT, we give generators and relations for the desired algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}), thus specifying it uniquely up to isomorphism. For completeness, a detailed description of the construction is given in Appendix B. The generators are written Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f), labelled by test functions f∈C0∞​(𝕄)f\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}) – for the moment this just a convenient way of writing them; there is no underlying field Φ⁡(x)\Phi(x) to be understood here. The relations imposed, for all test functions f,g∈C0∞​(𝕄)f,g\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}), are:

  1. SF1

    Linearity f↦Φ⁡(f)f\mapsto\Phi(f) is complex linear

  2. SF2

    Hermiticity Φ​(f)∗=Φ⁡(f¯)\Phi(f)^{*}=\Phi(\overline{f})

  3. SF3

    Field equation Φ⁡((□+m2)​f)=0\Phi((\Box+m^{2})f)=0

  4. SF4

    Covariant commutation relations [Φ⁡(f),Φ⁡(g)]=i​E​(f,g)​𝟙[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]=iE(f,g){\mathbb{1}}.

As a consequence of the identities in Exercise 13, SF4 is a covariant form of the equal time commutation relations; a nice way of seeing this directly is to follow the on-shell Peierls’ method [Pei52] to find a covariant Poisson bracket for the classical theory. The axioms we have just stated may be regarded as the result of applying Dirac’s quantisation rule to this bracket, with Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) regarded as the quantization of the observable

Ff​[ϕ]=∫f​ϕ​dvol𝕄F_{f}[\phi]=\int f\phi\,{\textrm{dvol}}_{\mathbb{M}} (27)

on a suitable solution space to the Klein–Gordon equation.

One should check, of course, that the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) is nontrivial. It is not too hard [though we will not do this here] to show that the underlying vector space of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) is isomorphic to the symmetric tensor vector space

ℂ⊕⨁n=1∞Q⊙n,Q=C0∞​(𝕄)/P​C0∞​(𝕄),\mathbb{C}\oplus\bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty}Q^{\odot n},\hskip 20.00003ptQ=C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})/PC_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}),

where P=□+m2P=\Box+m^{2} and ⊙\odot denotes a symmetrised tensor product. Therefore the nontriviality of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) reduces to the question of whether the quotient space QQ is nontrivial. The latter follows from the properties of the Green operators, which can be summarised in an exact sequence [BGP07]

0⟶C0∞​(𝕄)⟶PC0∞​(𝕄)⟶ECsc∞​(𝕄)⟶PCsc∞​(𝕄)⟶0,0\longrightarrow C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\longrightarrow}}C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle E}}{{\longrightarrow}}C^{\infty}_{\textit{sc}}(\mathbb{M})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\longrightarrow}}C^{\infty}_{\textit{sc}}(\mathbb{M})\longrightarrow 0, (28)

where the subscript s​csc denotes a space of functions with ‘spatially compact’ support, which means that they vanish in the causal complement of a compact set. Together with the isomorphism theorems for vector spaces, this gives

Q=C0∞​(𝕄)/im⁡P=C0∞​(𝕄)/ker⁡E≅im⁡E=ker⁡P={ϕ∈Csc∞​(𝕄):P​ϕ=0}=:Sol⁡(𝕄).Q=C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})/\im P=C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})/\ker E\cong\im E=\ker P=\{\phi\in C^{\infty}_{\textit{sc}}(\mathbb{M}):P\phi=0\}=:\Sol(\mathbb{M}). (29)

Thus QQ is isomorphic to the space of smooth Klein–Gordon solutions with spatially compact support, and is therefore nontrivial. Consequently, 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) is a nontrivial unital ∗*-algebra.

Now define, for each causally convex open bounded 𝒪⊂𝕄\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{M}, the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) to be the subalgebra of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) generated by elements Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) for f∈C0∞​(𝒪)f\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}), along with the unit 𝟙{\mathbb{1}}. Then it is clear that, if 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}, then 𝒜⁡(𝒪1)⊂𝒜⁡(𝒪2){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\subset{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}). Then properties A1, A2 are automatic. Next, because E⁡(f,g)=0E(f,g)=0 when ff and gg have causally disjoint support (as E​gEg is supported in the union of the causal future and past of supp⁡g\supp g) it is clear that all generators of 𝒜⁡(𝒪1){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) commute with all generators of 𝒜⁡(𝒪2){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}); hence A3 holds. Next, let ρ∈𝒫0\rho\in{\mathcal{P}}_{0}. Then the Poincaré covariance of □+m2\Box+m^{2} and EE can be used to show that the map of generators α⁡(ρ)​Φ​(f)=Φ⁡(ρ∗​f)\alpha(\rho)\Phi(f)=\Phi(\rho_{*}f), (ρ∗​f)​(x)=f⁡(ρ−1​(x))(\rho_{*}f)(x)=f(\rho^{-1}(x)), is compatible with the relations and extends to a well-defined unit-preserving ∗*-isomorphism

α⁡(ρ):𝒜⁡(𝕄)→𝒜⁡(𝕄).\alpha(\rho):{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})\to{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})\,. (30)

Clearly α⁡(ρ)\alpha(\rho) maps each 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) to 𝒜⁡(ρ​𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\rho\mathcal{O}); as we also have α⁡(σ)∘α⁡(ρ)=α⁡(σ∘ρ)\alpha(\sigma)\circ\alpha(\rho)=\alpha(\sigma\circ\rho), condition A4 holds.

Finally, let 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2} such that 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} contains a Cauchy surface of 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. Then any solution ϕ=E​f2\phi=Ef_{2} for f2∈C0∞​(𝒪2)f_{2}\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) can be written as ϕ=E​f1\phi=Ef_{1} for some f1∈C0∞​(𝒪1)f_{1}\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}_{1}). An explicit formula is

f1=P​χ​ϕf_{1}=P\chi\phi

where χ∈C∞​(𝒪2)\chi\in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) vanishes to the future of one Cauchy surface of 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} contained in 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and equals unity to the past of another (since 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} contains a Cauchy surface of 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}, it actually contains many of them). Then Φ⁡(f2)=Φ⁡(f1)\Phi(f_{2})=\Phi(f_{1}), which implies that 𝒜⁡(𝒪2)=𝒜⁡(𝒪1){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})={\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) as required by A5.

In fact this whole construction can be adapted to any globally hyperbolic spacetime, which is the setting in which (28) was proved [BGP07]. Here, we recall that a globally hyperbolic spacetime is a time-oriented Lorentzian spacetime containing a Cauchy surface.

Real scalar field with external source (van Hove encore)

Let ρ∈𝒟′​(𝕄)\rho\in{\mathscr{D}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}) be a distribution that is real in the sense ρ⁡(f)¯=ρ⁡(f¯)\overline{\rho(f)}=\rho(\overline{f}), and let ϕρ∈𝒟′​(𝕄)\phi_{\rho}\in{\mathscr{D}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}) be any weak solution to (□+m2)​ϕρ=−ρ(\Box+m^{2})\phi_{\rho}=-\rho.

The AQFT formulation of the real scalar field with external source ρ\rho is given in terms of the same algebras 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) as in the homogeneous case. The only difference is that we define smeared fields

Φρ​(f)=Φ⁡(f)+ϕρ​(f)​𝟙,\Phi_{\rho}(f)=\Phi(f)+\phi_{\rho}(f){\mathbb{1}},

where Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) are the generators used to construct 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) by SF1–SF4, and observe that they obey the algebraic relations

  1. vH1

    f↦Φρ​(f)f\mapsto\Phi_{\rho}(f) is complex linear

  2. vH2

    Φρ​(f)∗=Φρ​(f¯)\Phi_{\rho}(f)^{*}=\Phi_{\rho}(\overline{f})

  3. vH3

    Φρ​((□+m2)​f)+ρ⁡(f)​𝟙=0\Phi_{\rho}((\Box+m^{2})f)+\rho(f){\mathbb{1}}=0

  4. vH4

    [Φρ​(f),Φρ​(g)]=i​E​(f,g)​𝟙[\Phi_{\rho}(f),\Phi_{\rho}(g)]=iE(f,g){\mathbb{1}}

which are the relations that would be obtained from Dirac quantisation of the classical theory. Two remarks are in order:

  • •

    We see that the algebra is not so specific to the theory in hand – this is a general feature of AQFT: what is more interesting is how the local algebras fit together and how the elements can be labelled by fields.

  • •

    All the difficulties encountered in section 3 appear to have vanished. Actually, they have been moved into the question of the unitary (in)equivalence of representations of the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). The separation between the algebra and its representations makes for a clean conceptual viewpoint.

Weyl algebra

We return to the real scalar field and note two formal identities: first, that

(ei​Φ​(f))∗=e−i​Φ​(f)=ei​Φ​(−f)(e^{i\Phi(f)})^{*}=e^{-i\Phi(f)}=e^{i\Phi(-f)} (31)

if ff is real-valued; second, from the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula, that

ei​Φ​(f)ei​Φ​(g)=ei​Φ​(f)+i​Φ​(g)−[Φ⁡(f),Φ⁡(g)]/2=e−iE(f,g)/2ei​Φ​(f+g).e^{i\Phi(f)}e^{i\Phi(g)}=e^{i\Phi(f)+i\Phi(g)-[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]/2}=e^{-iE(f,g)/2}e^{i\Phi(f+g)}. (32)

As there is no topology on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) we cannot address any convergence questions, so these are to be understood as identities between formal power series in ff and gg. We may also note that Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) and E⁡(f,g)E(f,g) depend only on the equivalence classes of ff and gg in C0∞​(𝕄)/P​C0∞​(𝕄)≅Sol⁡(𝕄)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})/PC_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})\cong\Sol(\mathbb{M}). Moreover, the exponent in (32) is related to the symplectic product on the space of real-valued Klein–Gordon solutions, Solℝ⁡(𝕄)≅C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)/P​C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M})\cong C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R})/PC_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}) by

σ⁡([f],[g])=E⁡(f,g).\sigma([f],[g])=E(f,g). (33)

These considerations motivate the definition of a unital ∗*-algebra, generated by symbols 𝖶⁡([f]){\mathsf{W}}([f]) labelled by [f]∈C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)/P​C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)[f]\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R})/PC_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}) and satisfying relations mimicking (31) and (32). In fact, any real symplectic space (S,σ)(S,\sigma) determines a unital ∗*-algebra, generated by symbols 𝖶⁡(ϕ){\mathsf{W}}(\phi), ϕ∈S\phi\in S and satisfying the relations:

  1. W1

    𝖶​(ϕ)∗=𝖶⁡(−ϕ){\mathsf{W}}(\phi)^{*}={\mathsf{W}}(-\phi)

  2. W2

    𝖶(ϕ)𝖶(ϕ′)=e−iσ(ϕ,ϕ′)/2𝖶(ϕ+ϕ′){\mathsf{W}}(\phi){\mathsf{W}}(\phi^{\prime})=e^{-i\sigma(\phi,\phi^{\prime})/2}{\mathsf{W}}(\phi+\phi^{\prime}).

It is a remarkable fact that this algebra can be given a C∗C^{*}-norm and completed to form a C∗C^{*}-algebra in exactly one way (up to isomorphism) [BR97]. This is the Weyl algebra 𝒲⁡(S,σ){\mathcal{W}}(S,\sigma). In our case of interest S=C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)/P​C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)S=C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R})/PC_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}), the symplectic form is given by (33), and we will denote the corresponding Weyl algebra by 𝒲⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{W}}(\mathbb{M}) for short. As before, we can form local algebras by defining 𝒲⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{O}) as the C∗C^{*}-subalgebra generated by 𝖶⁡([f]){\mathsf{W}}([f])’s with supp⁡f⊂𝒪\supp f\subset\mathcal{O} and 𝒪\mathcal{O} being any causally convex open bounded subset of 𝕄\mathbb{M}.

Exercise 14.

In a general Weyl algebra 𝒲⁡(S,σ){\mathcal{W}}(S,\sigma), prove that 𝖶⁡(0)=𝟙{\mathsf{W}}(0)={\mathbb{1}}, the algebra unit.

It is worth pausing to examine the explicit construction of the Weyl algebra 𝒲⁡(S,σ){\mathcal{W}}(S,\sigma). Consider the (inseparable) Hilbert space ℋ=ℓ2​(S){\mathcal{H}}=\ell^{2}(S) of square-summable sequences a=(aϕ)a=(a_{\phi}) indexed by ϕ∈S\phi\in S, and define

(𝖶(ϕ′)a)ϕ=e−iσ(ϕ′,ϕ)/2aϕ+ϕ′.({\mathsf{W}}(\phi^{\prime})a)_{\phi}=e^{-i\sigma(\phi^{\prime},\phi)/2}a_{\phi+\phi^{\prime}}. (34)

Obviously the 𝖶⁡(ϕ){\mathsf{W}}(\phi)’s are all unitary. The Weyl algebra 𝒲⁡(S,σ){\mathcal{W}}(S,\sigma) is the closure of the ∗*-algebra generated by the 𝖶⁡(ϕ){\mathsf{W}}(\phi)’s in the norm topology on ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}), equipped with the operator norm.

Exercise 15.

Check that (34) implies 𝖶⁡(ϕ)=𝖶​(−ϕ)∗{\mathsf{W}}(\phi)={\mathsf{W}}(-\phi)^{*} and 𝖶(ϕ)𝖶(ϕ′)=e−iσ(ϕ,ϕ′)/2𝖶(ϕ+ϕ′){\mathsf{W}}(\phi){\mathsf{W}}(\phi^{\prime})=e^{-i\sigma(\phi,\phi^{\prime})/2}{\mathsf{W}}(\phi+\phi^{\prime}).

Exercise 16.

Let Ω∈ℓ2​(S)\Omega\in\ell^{2}(S) be the sequence (δϕ,0)(\delta_{\phi,0}), where

δϕ,0={1ϕ=00ϕ≠0.\delta_{\phi,0}=\begin{cases}1&\phi=0\\ 0&\phi\neq 0.\end{cases}

If ϕ≠ϕ′\phi\neq\phi^{\prime}, show that 𝖶⁡(ϕ)​Ω{\mathsf{W}}(\phi)\Omega and 𝖶⁡(ϕ′)​Ω{\mathsf{W}}(\phi^{\prime})\Omega are orthogonal and deduce that

‖𝖶⁡(ϕ)−𝖶⁡(ϕ′)‖=2.\|{\mathsf{W}}(\phi)-{\mathsf{W}}(\phi^{\prime})\|=2.

This shows that there are no nonconstant continuous curves in the Weyl algebra.

A corollary of the exercise is that one cannot differentiate λ↦𝖶⁡([λ​f])\lambda\mapsto{\mathsf{W}}([\lambda f]) within the Weyl algebra in the hope of recovering a smeared field operator, nor can we exponentiate i​Φ​(f)i\Phi(f) within the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) to obtain a Weyl operator. The heuristic relationship 𝖶⁡([f])=ei​Φ​(f){\mathsf{W}}([f])=e^{i\Phi(f)} does not hold literally in either of these algebras.

Exercise 17.

Show that the GNS representation of the (abstract) Weyl algebra over symplectic space (S,σ)(S,\sigma) induced by the tracial state ωtr​(𝖶⁡(ϕ))=δϕ,0\omega_{\text{tr}}({\mathsf{W}}(\phi))=\delta_{\phi,0} coincides with the concrete construction of a representation on ℋ=ℓ2​(S)\mathcal{H}=\ell^{2}(S) given earlier, with the GNS vector Ωtr=(δϕ,0)\Omega_{\text{tr}}=(\delta_{\phi,0}), i.e., ωtr​(A)=⟨Ωtr|A​Ωtr⟩\omega_{\text{tr}}(A)=\langle\Omega_{\text{tr}}|A\Omega_{\text{tr}}\rangle.

Complex scalar field

The algebra of the free complex scalar field 𝒞⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{M}) may be generated by symbols Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) (f∈C0∞​(𝕄)f\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M})) subject to the relations

  1. CF1

    Linearity f↦Φ⁡(f)f\mapsto\Phi(f) is complex linear

  2. CF2

    Field equation Φ⁡((□+m2)​f)=0\Phi((\Box+m^{2})f)=0

  3. CF3

    Covariant commutation relations [Φ⁡(f),Φ⁡(g)]=0[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]=0 and [Φ​(f)∗,Φ⁡(g)]=i​E​(f¯,g)​𝟙[\Phi(f)^{*},\Phi(g)]=iE(\bar{f},g){\mathbb{1}}.

It is also usual to write Φ⋆​(f):=Φ​(f¯)∗\Phi^{\star}(f):=\Phi(\bar{f})^{*}, so that f↦Φ⋆​(f)f\mapsto\Phi^{\star}(f) is also complex-linear. This algebra admits a family of automorphisms ηα\eta_{\alpha} given on the generators by

ηα​(Φ⁡(f))=e−i​α​Φ​(f),\eta_{\alpha}(\Phi(f))=e^{-i\alpha}\Phi(f), (35)

corresponding to a global U⁡(1)U(1) gauge symmetry of the classical complex field.

Exercise 18.

Check that (35) extends to a well-defined automorphism for each α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}. Show also that there is an isomorphism between 𝒞⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{M}) and the algebraic tensor product 𝒜⁡(𝕄)⊗𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})\otimes{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) of two copies of the real scalar field algebra (with the same mass mm) given on generators by

Φ⁡(f)↦12​(Φr​(f)⊗𝟙+i​𝟙⊗Φr​(f)),f∈C0∞​(𝕄),\Phi(f)\mapsto\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\Phi_{r}(f)\otimes{\mathbb{1}}+i{\mathbb{1}}\otimes\Phi_{r}(f)\right),\hskip 20.00003ptf\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}),

where we temporarily use Φr​(f)\Phi_{r}(f) to denote the generators of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). In this sense, the complex field is simply two independent real scalar fields.

We may identify local algebras 𝒞⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{O}) in the same way as before, and within each of these, identify the subalgebra 𝒞obs​(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O}) consisting of all elements of 𝒞⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{O}) that are invariant under the global U⁡(1)U(1) gauge action. These are the local observable algebras.

The reader may notice that the real scalar field admits a global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge symmetry generated by Φ⁡(f)↦−Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f)\mapsto-\Phi(f), and that the theory of two independent real scalar fields with the same mass admits an O⁡(2)O(2) gauge symmetry, of which the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry corresponds to the S​O​(2)SO(2) subgroup. Why, then, do we not restrict the observable algebra of the real scalar field, or further restrict the observable algebras of the complex field? The answer is simply that these are physical choices. The U⁡(1)U(1) gauge invariance of the complex scalar field is related to charge conservation, while the additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry in the isomorphism O⁡(2)≅U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2O(2)\cong U(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} corresponds to charge reversal. If the theory is used to model a charge that is conserved in nature, but for which states of opposite charge can be physically distinguished, then the correct approach is to proceed as we have done.

Dirac field

One can proceed in a similar way to define an algebra ℱ⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{F}}(\mathbb{M}) with generators Ψ⁡(u)\Psi(u) and Ψ+​(v)\Psi^{+}(v) labelled by cospinor and spinor test functions respectively, and with relations abstracted from standard QFT (this is left as an exercise). However, the resulting local algebras ℱ⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{O}) do not obey Einstein causality – if uu and vv are spacelike separated then Ψ⁡(u)\Psi(u) and Ψ+​(v)\Psi^{+}(v) anticommute. Of course we do not expect to be able to measure a smeared spinor field by itself, and what one can do instead is consider algebras generated by second degree products of the spinor and cospinor fields, labelled by (co)spinor test functions in supported in 𝒪\mathcal{O}. The resulting algebras 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) then obey the axioms A1–A5.

Meanwhile, the algebras ℱ⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{O}) obey A1, A2, A4, A5 and a graded version of A3. We describe them as constituting local field algebras, to emphasise the fact that they contain elements carrying the interpretation of smeared unobservable fields. We will come back to the discussion of ℱ⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{O}) and their relation to 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) in section 8 on superselection sectors.

4.3 Quasifree states for the free scalar field

We have seen how local algebras for the free scalar field may be constructed. As emphasised in Sec. 2.2, however, this is only half of the data needed for a physical theory: we also need some states, and (for many purposes) the corresponding GNS representations. These are nontrivial problems in general: one needs to fix the value of ω⁡(A)\omega(A) and verify the positivity condition that ω⁡(A∗​A)≥0\omega(A^{*}A)\geq 0 for every element A∈𝒜⁡(𝕄)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}); furthermore, while the GNS representation is fairly explicit, it evidently involves a lot of work to do it by hand.

Fortunately, in the case of free fields, there is a special family of quasifree states where quite explicit constructions can be given. In particular, these states are determined by their two-point functions and all the conditions required of a state can be expressed in those terms. Moreover, the eventual GNS Hilbert space is a Fock space, and the smeared field operators in the representation may be given by explicit formulae. It is important to note that these include representations that are unitarily inequivalent to the representation built on the standard vacuum state. Once again, many of the arguments we will use carry over directly to curved spacetimes.

Let WW be any bilinear form on C0∞​(𝕄)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}) obeying

W⁡(f,g)−W⁡(g,f)=i​E​(f,g),∀f,g∈C0∞​(𝕄)W(f,g)-W(g,f)=iE(f,g),\hskip 20.00003pt\forall f,g\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}) (36)

and which induces a positive semidefinite sesquilinear form on Sol⁡(𝕄)\Sol(\mathbb{M}) by the formula

w⁡(E​f,E​g)=W⁡(f¯,g),∀f,g∈C0∞​(𝕄).w(Ef,Eg)=W(\overline{f},g),\hskip 20.00003pt\forall f,g\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}).

In particular, WW must be a weak bisolution to the Klein–Gordon equation so that ww is well-defined.

Exercise 19.

Check that the positivity condition W⁡(f¯,f)≥0W(\bar{f},f)\geq 0 implies that W⁡(f,g)¯=W⁡(g¯,f¯)\overline{W(f,g)}=W(\bar{g},\bar{f}). Also derive the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

|Im⁡w⁡(ϕ,ϕ′)|2≤w⁡(ϕ,ϕ)​w​(ϕ′,ϕ′),ϕ,ϕ′∈Sol⁡(𝕄).|\Im w(\phi,\phi^{\prime})|^{2}\leq w(\phi,\phi)w(\phi^{\prime},\phi^{\prime}),\hskip 20.00003pt\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\Sol(\mathbb{M}). (37)

Under the above conditions, it may be proved (cf. Prop 3.1 in [KW91]) that there is a complex Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and a real-linear map K:Solℝ⁡(𝕄)→ℋK:\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M})\to{\mathcal{H}} so that K​Solℝ⁡(𝕄)+i​K​Solℝ⁡(𝕄)K\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M})+iK\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}) is dense in ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and

⟨K​E​f|K​E​g⟩ℋ=W⁡(f,g),f,g∈C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ).\langle KEf|KEg\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=W(f,g),\hskip 20.00003ptf,g\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}). (38)

(These structures are unique up to unitary equivalence.)

The full construction is essentially explicit, but slightly involved. However, there is a particularly simple and interesting case, arising when the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (37) is saturated, i.e.,

supϕ′≠0|Im⁡w⁡(ϕ,ϕ′)|2w⁡(ϕ,ϕ)​w​(ϕ′,ϕ′)=1for all 0≠ϕ∈Solℝ⁡(𝕄),\sup_{\phi^{\prime}\neq 0}\frac{|\Im w(\phi,\phi^{\prime})|^{2}}{w(\phi,\phi)w(\phi^{\prime},\phi^{\prime})}=1\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for all $0\neq\phi\in\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M})$}, (39)

where the supremum is taken over nonzero elements of Solℝ⁡(𝕄)\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}). This occurs if and only if the quasifree state constructed below is pure. Under these circumstances, ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is first defined as a real Hilbert space by completing Solℝ⁡(𝕄)\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}) in the norm ‖ϕ‖w=w​(ϕ,ϕ)1/2\|\phi\|_{w}=w(\phi,\phi)^{1/2} with inner product ⟨ϕ1|ϕ2⟩w=Re⁡w⁡(ϕ1,ϕ2)\langle\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}\rangle_{w}=\Re w(\phi_{1},\phi_{2}). Due to (39), ℋ{\mathcal{H}} carries an isometry JJ defined so that

Im⁡w⁡(ϕ1,ϕ2)=⟨ϕ1|J​ϕ2⟩w,ϕi∈ℋ,\Im w(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})=\langle\phi_{1}|J\phi_{2}\rangle_{w},\hskip 20.00003pt\phi_{i}\in{\mathcal{H}},

and which fulfils the conditions J2=−𝟙J^{2}=-{\mathbb{1}}, J†=−JJ^{\dagger}=-J. Hence JJ is a complex structure on ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, and we can make ℋ{\mathcal{H}} into a complex Hilbert space in which multiplication by ii is (annoyingly) implemented by −J-J and the inner product is

⟨ϕ1|ϕ2⟩ℋ=⟨ϕ1|ϕ2⟩w+i​⟨ϕ1|J​ϕ2⟩w.\langle\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}\rangle_{w}+i\langle\phi_{1}|J\phi_{2}\rangle_{w}.

(See Appendix A for more details.) The map KK is just the natural inclusion of Solℝ⁡(𝕄)\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}) in ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and it is clear that K​Solℝ​(𝕄)K\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}) is dense in ℋ{\mathcal{H}} (hence K​Solℝ⁡(𝕄)+i​K​Solℝ⁡(𝕄)K\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M})+iK\Sol_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{M}) is also dense). Verification of (38) is left as an exercise.

Returning to the general case, it may be shown that there is a state on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) given, as a formal series in ff, by

ω(ei​Φ​(f))=e−W(f,f)/2,f∈C0∞(𝕄;ℝ).\omega(e^{i\Phi(f)})=e^{-W(f,f)/2},\hskip 20.00003ptf\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}). (40)

Expanding each side of (40) in powers of ff, and equating terms at each order, all expectation values of the form ω⁡(Φ​(f)n)\omega(\Phi(f)^{n}) are fixed. Arbitrary expectation values may then be formed using multilinear polarisation identities (see e.g., [Tho14] and references therein) and linearity. It may be shown that all odd nn-point functions vanish, while

ω(Φ(f1)⋯Φ(f2​n))=∑G∈𝒢2​n∏e∈GW(fs⁡(e),ft⁡(e)),\omega(\Phi(f_{1})\cdots\Phi(f_{2n}))=\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}_{2n}}\prod_{e\in G}W(f_{s(e)},f_{t(e)}),

where 𝒢2​n\mathcal{G}_{2n} is the set of directed graphs with vertices labelled 1,…,2​n1,\ldots,2n, such that each vertex is met by exactly one edge and the source and target of each edge obey s⁡(e)<t⁡(e)s(e)<t(e). An example for n=4n=4 is given in Figure 2. Another characterisation of the nn-point functions is that all the truncated nn-point functions vanish for n≠0,2n\neq 0,2. This type of state is described as quasifree.

Exercise 20.

Using (40), show that ω⁡(Φ​(f)2​n+1)=0\omega(\Phi(f)^{2n+1})=0 for all n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, while

ω⁡(Φ​(f)2​n)=(2​n−1)!!​W​(f,f)n,∀n∈ℕ0.\omega(\Phi(f)^{2n})=(2n-1)!!\,W(f,f)^{n},\hskip 20.00003pt\forall n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}.

Deduce that the sequence μn=ω⁡(Φ​(f)n)\mu_{n}=\omega(\Phi(f)^{n}) satisfies the growth conditions in the Hamburger moment theorem. Therefore these are the moments of at most one probability measure – which is of course a Gaussian probability distribution.

Although we have called ω\omega a state, it is not yet clear that it has the required positivity property. This is most easily justified by noting that there is an explicit Hilbert space representation of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) containing a unit vector whose expectation values match those of ω\omega. To be specific, the Hilbert space is the bosonic Fock space

𝔉⁡(ℋ)=⨁n=0∞ℋ⊙n{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}})=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot n} (41)

over ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, on which the field is represented according to the formula

πω​(Φ⁡(f))=a⁡(K​E​f)+a∗​(K​E​f),f∈C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ),\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f))=a(KEf)+a^{*}(KEf),\hskip 20.00003ptf\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}), (42)

and

πω​(Φ⁡(f)):=πω​(Φ⁡(Re⁡f))+i​πω​(Φ⁡(Im⁡f))\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f)):=\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(\Re f))+i\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(\Im f))

for general complex-valued f∈C0∞​(𝕄)f\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}). Here a⁡(ϕ)a(\phi) and a∗​(ψ)a^{*}(\psi) are the annihilation and creation operators on the Fock space which obey the CCRs

[a⁡(ϕ),a∗​(ψ)]=⟨ϕ|ψ⟩ℋ​𝟙,ϕ,ψ∈ℋ,[a(\phi),a^{*}(\psi)]=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}{\mathbb{1}},\hskip 20.00003pt\phi,\psi\in{\mathcal{H}}, (43)

on a suitable dense domain in 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}) (note that aa is antilinear in its argument, and that a⁡(ϕ)=a∗​(ϕ)∗a(\phi)=a^{*}(\phi)^{*}). Readers unfamiliar with the basis-independent notation used here should refer to Appendix C.

We will not give a detailed proof of the claims (40–43), which would require consideration of operator domains. At the level of formal calculation, however, it is easily checked that these operators do indeed lead to a representation of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}).

Exercise 21.

Verify formally that f↦πω​(Φ​(f))f\mapsto\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f)) is ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear, obeys the field equation in the sense πω​(Φ​(P​f))=0\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(Pf))=0, and is hermitian in the sense that πω​(Φ⁡(f))∗=πω​(Φ⁡(f¯))\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f))^{*}=\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(\overline{f})).

For the CCRs, we compute

[πω​(Φ⁡(f)),πω​(Φ⁡(g))]=(⟨K​E​f|K​E​g⟩ℋ−⟨K​E​g|K​E​f⟩ℋ)​𝟙=(W⁡(f,g)−W⁡(g,f))​𝟙=i​E​(f,g)​𝟙,[\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f)),\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(g))]=\left(\langle KEf|KEg\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle KEg|KEf\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\right){\mathbb{1}}=\left(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\right){\mathbb{1}}=iE(f,g){\mathbb{1}},

using (43), (38) and (36). Finally, it may be verified that the Fock vacuum vector Ωω\Omega_{\omega} satisfies

⟨Ωω|πω(Φ(f1))⋯πω(Φ(fn))Ωω⟩=ω(Φ(f1)⋯Φ(fn)).\langle\Omega_{\omega}|\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f_{1}))\cdots\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f_{n}))\Omega_{\omega}\rangle=\omega(\Phi(f_{1})\cdots\Phi(f_{n})).

Consequently, ω\omega is seen to be a vector state on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) and the quadruple (𝔉⁡(ℋ),𝒟ω,πω,Ωω)({\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}),{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega},\pi_{\omega},\Omega_{\omega}) is its GNS representation, where the dense domain 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} consists of finite linear combinations of finite products of operators a∗​(K​E​f)a^{*}(KEf) acting on Ωω\Omega_{\omega}.

The ‘one-particle space’ ℋ{\mathcal{H}} may be interpreted as follows. By (42), we see that

πω​(Φ⁡(f))​Ωω=a∗​(K​E​f)​Ωω=(0,K​E​f,0,…)∈𝔉⁡(ℋ),\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f))\Omega_{\omega}=a^{*}(KEf)\Omega_{\omega}=(0,KEf,0,\ldots)\in{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}),

which is an eigenstate of NN with unit eigenvalue. Elements of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} can be identified with (complex linear combinations of) vectors generated from Ωω\Omega_{\omega} by a single application of the field. Due to assumption SF3, these vectors may be identified with certain complex-valued solutions to the field equation, which may be regarded as wavepackets of ‘positive frequency modes’ relative to a decomposition induced by the choice of quasifree state.

Examples

Wβ​(f,g)=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​12​ω​(f^​(−k)​g^​(k)1−e−β​ω+f^​(k)​g^​(−k)eβ​ω−1).W_{\beta}(f,g)=\int\frac{d^{3}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{2\omega}\left(\frac{\hat{f}(-k)\hat{g}(k)}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}+\frac{\hat{f}(k)\hat{g}(-k)}{e^{\beta\omega}-1}\right).
