(Kβ​ϕ)​(k)=(K​ϕ)​(k)1−e−β​ω⊕(K​ϕ)​(k)¯eβ​ω−1(K_{\beta}\phi)(k)=\frac{(K\phi)(k)}{\sqrt{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}}\oplus\frac{\overline{(K\phi)(k)}}{\sqrt{e^{\beta\omega}-1}}

(remember that KβK_{\beta} only has to be real-linear!). The range of Kβ​EK_{\beta}E is not dense in ℋβ{\mathcal{H}}_{\beta}, but its complex span is, reflecting the fact that the thermal states are mixed.

Exercise 22.

Check that the analogue of (38) holds for ℋβ{\mathcal{H}}_{\beta}, KβK_{\beta} and WβW_{\beta}.

A nice feature of the algebraic approach is that, while the representations corresponding to the vacuum and thermal states are unitarily inequivalent, they can be treated ‘democratically’ as states on the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). There are many other quasifree states; indeed one can start with any state and construct its ‘liberation’, the quasifree state with the same two-point function.

All quasifree representations carry a representation π~ω\tilde{\pi}_{\omega} of the Weyl algebra as well, so that

π~ω​(𝖶⁡([f]))=ei​πω​(Φ⁡(f))\tilde{\pi}_{\omega}({\mathsf{W}}([f]))=e^{i\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f))}

and also

πω​(Φ⁡(f))=1i​dd​λ​𝖶​([λ​f])|λ=0.\pi_{\omega}(\Phi(f))=\left.\frac{1}{i}\frac{d}{d\lambda}{\mathsf{W}}([\lambda f])\right|_{\lambda=0}.

Remember that these relationships cannot hold literally either in 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) or 𝒲⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{W}}(\mathbb{M}), but here we see that they do hold in (sufficiently regular) representations.

Summarising, the quasifree states provide a class of states for which explicit Hilbert space representations may be given with the familiar Fock space structure, and in which the Weyl operators and smeared field operators are related as just described.

5 The spectrum condition and Reeh–Schlieder theorem

In this section we begin to draw general conclusions about the properties of QFT in the AQFT framework, proceeding from the basic axioms and additional requirements that will be introduced along the way. We shall emphasise features that distinguish QFT from quantum mechanics. The starting point is a more detailed discussion of the action of Poincaré transformations.

5.1 The spectrum condition

Assumption A4 required that the Poincaré group should act by automorphisms of 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}). An important question concerning Hilbert space representations of the theory is whether or not these automorphisms are unitarily implemented, i.e., whether there are unitaries U⁡(ρ)U(\rho) on the representation Hilbert space such that

π⁡(α⁡(ρ)​A)=U⁡(ρ)​π​(A)​U​(ρ)−1.\pi(\alpha(\rho)A)=U(\rho)\pi(A)U(\rho)^{-1}.

In such cases, we say that the representation is Poincaré covariant. As we now show, the GNS representation of a Poincaré invariant state ω\omega is always Poincaré covariant. Here, Poincaré invariance of ω\omega means that

ω⁡(α⁡(ρ)​A)=ω⁡(A),∀A∈𝒜⁡(𝕄),ρ∈𝒫0\omega(\alpha(\rho)A)=\omega(A),\hskip 20.00003pt\forall A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}),~\rho\in{\mathcal{P}}_{0}

(written equivalently as α​(ρ)∗​ω=ω\alpha(\rho)^{*}\omega=\omega for all ρ∈𝒫0\rho\in{\mathcal{P}}_{0}, with the star denoting the dual map). Of course, the same question can be asked of any automorphism or automorphism group on a ∗*-algebra.

Theorem 23.

Let α\alpha be an automorphism of a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. If a state ω\omega on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is invariant under α\alpha, i.e., α∗​ω=ω\alpha^{*}\omega=\omega, then α\alpha is unitarily implemented in the GNS representation of ω\omega by a unitary that leaves the GNS vector invariant. Any group of automorphisms leaving ω\omega invariant is unitarily represented in ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}.

Proof.

Observing that ω⁡(α​(A)∗​α​(A))=(α∗​ω)​(A∗​A)=ω⁡(A∗​A)\omega(\alpha(A)^{*}\alpha(A))=(\alpha^{*}\omega)(A^{*}A)=\omega(A^{*}A), we see that α\alpha maps the GNS ideal ℐω{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega} to itself. Therefore the formula

U⁡[A]=[α⁡(A)]U[A]=[\alpha(A)]

gives a well-defined map UU from the GNS domain 𝒟ω{\mathscr{D}}_{\omega} to itself, which fixes the GNS vector Ωω=[𝟙]\Omega_{\omega}=[{\mathbb{1}}] and is obviously invertible (consider α−1\alpha^{-1}). Now

⟨U⁡[A]​|U⁡[B]⟩=ω⁡(α​(A)∗​α​(A))=ω⁡(A∗​A)=⟨[A]|​[B]⟩,\langle U[A]|U[B]\rangle=\omega(\alpha(A)^{*}\alpha(A))=\omega(A^{*}A)=\langle[A]|[B]\rangle,

so UU is a densely defined invertible isometry, and therefore extends uniquely to a unitary on ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}. The calculation

πω(α(A))[B]=[α(A)B]=[α(Aα−1(B))]=U[Aα−1(B))]=Uπω(A)[α−1B]=Uπω(A)U−1[B]\pi_{\omega}(\alpha(A))[B]=[\alpha(A)B]=[\alpha(A\alpha^{-1}(B))]=U[A\alpha^{-1}(B))]=U\pi_{\omega}(A)[\alpha^{-1}B]=U\pi_{\omega}(A)U^{-1}[B]

shows that UU implements α\alpha.

If β\beta is another automorphism leaving ω\omega invariant, let VV be its unitary implementation as above. Then

U​V​[A]=[α⁡(β⁡(A))]=[(α∘β)​(A)]UV[A]=[\alpha(\beta(A))]=[(\alpha\circ\beta)(A)]

shows that U​VUV implements α∘β\alpha\circ\beta. ∎

Among other things, this result may be applied to states that are translationally invariant. Thermal equilibrium states, for example, are spatially homogeoneous but not Poincaré invariant because they have a definite rest frame. Although typical states are not translationally invariant, many interesting states are in a suitable sense local deviations from such invariant states. Even so, not all invariant states are physically acceptable. One way of doing narrowing the field is to require the spectrum condition:

Definition 24.

Let ω\omega be a translationally invariant state so that the unitary implementation of the translation group U⁡(x)U(x) is strongly continuous, i.e., the map x↦U⁡(x)​ψx\mapsto U(x)\psi is continuous from ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} to ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega} for each fixed ψ∈ℋω\psi\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}, where x=(x0,…,x3)∈ℝ4x=(x^{0},\ldots,x^{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{4}. By Stone’s theorem, there are four commuting self-adjoint operators PμP^{\mu} such that (lowering the index using the metric)

U⁡(x)=ei​Pμ​xμ.U(x)=e^{iP_{\mu}x^{\mu}}.

To any (Borel) subset Δ⊂ℝ4\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{4} we may assign a projection operator E⁡(Δ)E(\Delta) corresponding to the binary test of whether the result of 44-momentum measurement PμP^{\mu} would be found to lie in Δ\Delta. The assignment Δ↦E⁡(Δ)\Delta\mapsto E(\Delta) is a projection-valued measure, and in fact one can write

U⁡(x)=∫ei​pμ​xμ​𝑑E​(p∙).U(x)=\int e^{ip_{\mu}x^{\mu}}dE(p^{\bullet}).

The state ω\omega is said to satisfy the spectrum condition if the support of EE lies in the closed forward cone V+¯={p∙∈ℝ4:pμpμ≥0,p0≥0}\overline{V^{+}}=\{p^{\bullet}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}:p^{\mu}p_{\mu}\geq 0,~p^{0}\geq 0\}, i.e.,

supp⁡E⊂V+¯.\supp E\subset\overline{V^{+}}.

This is sometimes expressed by saying that the joint spectrum of the momentum operators PμP^{\mu} lies in V+¯\overline{V^{+}}.

An important consequence of the spectrum condition is that the definition of U⁡(x)U(x) can be extended to complex vectors x∈ℝ4+i​V+x\in\mathbb{R}^{4}+iV^{+}, with analytic dependence on xx: to be precise, U⁡(x)U(x) is strongly continuous on ℝ4+i​V+¯\mathbb{R}^{4}+i\overline{V^{+}} and holomorphic on ℝ4+i​V+\mathbb{R}^{4}+i\,V^{+}, where V+=int​V+¯V^{+}=\text{int}\overline{V^{+}}.

One can check that the usual vacuum and thermal states of the free field obey the spectrum condition. More generally, we will make the following definition:

Definition 25.

A vacuum state1010 10 The term ‘vacuum’ is used in various ways by various authors, differing, for example, on whether Poincaré invariance is required as well. Somewhat remarkably, there is an algebraic criterion on the state that implies translational invariance, the spectrum condition and (if the state is pure) that the there is no other translationally invariant vector state in its GNS representation. See [Ara99]. is a translationally invariant state obeying the spectrum condition, whose GNS vector is the unique translationally invariant vector (up to scalar multiples) in the GNS Hilbert space. The corresponding GNS representation is called the vacuum representation.

5.2 The Reeh–Schlieder theorem

We come to some general results that show how different QFT is from quantum mechanics. For simplicity, suppose that the theory is given in terms of C∗C^{*}-algebras. Let Ω\Omega be the GNS vector of a state obeying the spectrum condition (we drop the ω\omega subscripts). Suppose the theory obeys the following condition:

  1. A6

    Weak additivity
    For any causally convex open region 𝒪\mathcal{O}, π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝕄))\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})) is contained in the weak closure1111 11 A sequence of operators converges in the weak topology, w-​limAn=A\text{w-}\lim A_{n}=A, if ⟨ψ⁡|An​φ⟩→⟨ψ|​A​φ⟩\langle\psi|A_{n}\varphi\rangle\to\langle\psi|A\varphi\rangle for all vectors ψ\psi and φ\varphi. of ℬ𝒪{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{O}}, the ∗*-algebra generated by the algebras π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪+x))\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}+x)) as xx runs over ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}.

Weak additivity asserts that arbitrary observables can be built as limits of algebraic combinations of translates of observables in any given region 𝒪\mathcal{O} (as one would expect in a quantum field theory). In combination with the spectrum condition it has a striking consequence. Our proof is based on that of [Ara99].

Theorem 26 (Reeh–Schlieder).

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be any causally convex bounded open region. Then (a) vectors of the form A​ΩA\Omega for A∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪))A\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) are dense in ℋ{\mathcal{H}}; (b) if A∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪))A\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) annihilates the vacuum, A​Ω=0A\Omega=0, then A=0A=0.

Part (a) says that Ω\Omega is cyclic for every local algebra; part (b) that it is also separating. The existence of a cyclic and separating vector on a (von Neumann) algebra is the starting point of Tomita–Takesaki theory (see, e.g., [BR87]).

These are quite remarkable statements: if a local element of 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) corresponds to an operation that can be performed in 𝒪\mathcal{O}, it seems that we can produce any state of the theory up to arbitrarily small errors by operations in any small region anywhere. To give an extreme example: by making a local operation in a laboratory on earth one could in principle modify the state of the theory to one approximating a situation in which there is a starship behind the moon, if such things can be modelled by the theory (e.g., as a complicated state of the standard model). It is an expression of how deeply entangled states in QFT typically are.

Proof.

(a) Suppose to the contrary that the set of vectors mentioned is not dense. Then it has a nontrivial orthogonal complement, so there is a nonzero vector Ψ∈ℋ\Psi\in{\mathcal{H}} such that

⟨Ψ|A​Ω⟩=0,∀A∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪)).\langle\Psi|A\Omega\rangle=0,\hskip 20.00003pt\forall A\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})).

Now let 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} be a slightly smaller region with 𝒪1¯⊂𝒪\overline{\mathcal{O}_{1}}\subset\mathcal{O}. For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and any Q1,…,Qn∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})) we have U⁡(x)​Qi​U​(x)−1∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪))U(x)Q_{i}U(x)^{-1}\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) for sufficiently small |x||x|, whereupon

⟨Ψ|U(x1)Q1U(x2−x1)Q2U(x3−x2)⋯U(xn−xn−1)QnΩ⟩=0\langle\Psi|U(x_{1})Q_{1}U(x_{2}-x_{1})Q_{2}U(x_{3}-x_{2})\cdots U(x_{n}-x_{n-1})Q_{n}\Omega\rangle=0 (44)

for sufficiently small x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. By what was said above, the function

F:(ζ1,…,ζn)↦⟨Ψ|U(ζ1)Q1U(ζ2)Q2⋯U(ζn)QnΩ⟩F:(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{n})\mapsto\langle\Psi|U(\zeta_{1})Q_{1}U(\zeta_{2})Q_{2}\cdots U(\zeta_{n})Q_{n}\Omega\rangle

is a continuous function on (ℝ4)n(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n} extending to an holomorphic function in (ℝ4+i​V+)n⊂(ℂ4)n(\mathbb{R}^{4}+iV^{+})^{n}\subset(\mathbb{C}^{4})^{n}, whose boundary value on (ℝ4)n(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n} moreover vanishes in some neighbourhood of the origin. The ‘edge of the wedge’ theorem [SW00, Vla66] implies that FF vanishes identically in its domain of holomorphicity, which means that the boundary value also vanishes identically. This means that (44) holds for all xix_{i}, or put another way, that

⟨Ψ|ℬ𝒪​Ω⟩=0\langle\Psi|{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{O}}\Omega\rangle=0

where ℬ𝒪{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{O}} is the algebra generated by the algebras π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪1+x))\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}+x)) for x∈ℝ4x\in\mathbb{R}^{4}. By weak additivity, we now know that ⟨Ψ|π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝕄))​Ω⟩=0\langle\Psi|\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}))\Omega\rangle=0. But Ωω\Omega_{\omega} is cyclic, so Ψ=0\Psi=0. This proves the first assertion. For the second, suppose that A∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))A\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})) annihilates Ω\Omega. Choose 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} causally disjoint from 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}, and note that for each ψ∈ℋ\psi\in{\mathcal{H}} and all B∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪2))B\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})) we have

⟨A∗​ψ|B​Ω⟩=⟨ψ|A​B​Ω⟩=⟨ψ|B​A​Ω⟩=0\langle A^{*}\psi|B\Omega\rangle=\langle\psi|AB\Omega\rangle=\langle\psi|BA\Omega\rangle=0

using Einstein causality. By the first part of the theorem, A∗​ψA^{*}\psi is orthogonal to a dense set and therefore vanishes; as ψ∈ℋ\psi\in{\mathcal{H}} is arbitrary we have A∗=0A^{*}=0 and hence A=0A=0. ∎

Corollary 27.

All nontrivial sharp local binary tests (with possible outcomes ‘success’ or ‘failure’) have a nonzero success probability in the vacuum state. (All local detectors exhibit ‘dark counts’).

Proof.

A binary test can be represented by a projector PP, with ‘failure’ corresponding to its kernel. Suppose P∈π⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪))P\in\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) is a projector with vanishing vacuum expectation value, i.e., a zero success probability. Then

‖P​Ω‖2=⟨P​Ω|P​Ω⟩=⟨Ω|P​Ω⟩=0,\|P\Omega\|^{2}=\langle P\Omega|P\Omega\rangle=\langle\Omega|P\Omega\rangle=0,

so P​Ω=0P\Omega=0 and hence P=0P=0 by the Reeh–Schlieder theorem (b). ∎

Corollary 28.

For every pair of local regions 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} there are vacuum correlations between 𝒜⁡(𝒪1){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) and 𝒜⁡(𝒪2){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) (assuming dimℋ≥1\dim{\mathcal{H}}\geq 1).

Proof.

For suppose to the contrary that there are states ωi\omega_{i} on 𝒜⁡(𝒪i){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{i}) such that

⟨Ω|π⁡(A1)​π​(A2)​Ω⟩=ω1​(A1)​ω2​(A2)Ai∈𝒜⁡(𝒪i).\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{1})\pi(A_{2})\Omega\rangle=\omega_{1}(A_{1})\omega_{2}(A_{2})\hskip 20.00003ptA_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{i}).

By setting A1=𝟙A_{1}={\mathbb{1}}, and then repeating for A2A_{2}, this implies

⟨Ω|π⁡(A1)​π​(A2)​Ω⟩=⟨Ω|π⁡(A1)​Ω⟩​⟨Ω|π⁡(A2)​Ω⟩Ai∈𝒜⁡(𝒪i)\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{1})\pi(A_{2})\Omega\rangle=\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{1})\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{2})\Omega\rangle\hskip 20.00003ptA_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{i})

Fixing A2A_{2} and letting A1A_{1} vary in 𝒜⁡(𝒪1){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}), the Reeh–Schlieder theorem gives

π⁡(A2)​Ω=⟨Ω|π⁡(A2)​Ω⟩​Ω,A2∈𝒜⁡(𝒪2)\pi(A_{2})\Omega=\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{2})\Omega\rangle\Omega,\hskip 20.00003ptA_{2}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})

which contradicts the Reeh–Schlieder theorem (a) unless dimℋ=1\dim{\mathcal{H}}=1. ∎

The correlations indicated by Corollary 28 become small at spacelike separation due to the cluster property (a general feature of vacuum states in AQFT), which implies

⟨Ω|π⁡(A1)​π​(α⁡(x)​A2)​Ω⟩→⟨Ω|π⁡(A1)​Ω⟩​⟨Ω|π⁡(A2)​Ω⟩\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{1})\pi(\alpha(x)A_{2})\Omega\rangle\to\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{1})\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\pi(A_{2})\Omega\rangle

as x→∞x\to\infty in spacelike directions, with exponentially fast convergence if the theory has a mass gap, i.e., σ⁡(P⋅P)⊂{0}∪[M2,∞)\sigma(P\cdot P)\subset\{0\}\cup[M^{2},\infty) for some M>0M>0. See [Ara99, §4.3-4.4]. The Reeh–Schlieder theorem does not present a very practical method for constructing starships.

6 Local von Neumann algebras and their universal type

So far, we have encountered AQFTs given in terms of ∗*-algebras or C∗C^{*}-algebras. The theory is considerably enriched when expressed in terms of von Neumann algebras.

Consider any net of local C∗C^{*}-algebras 𝒪↦𝒜⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{O}\mapsto{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) obeying A1–A5. Given any state ω\omega on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}), form its GNS representation. For any open bounded causally convex 𝒪⊂𝕄\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{M} we can define an algebra

𝔐ω​(𝒪):=πω​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′,{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}):=\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime},

namely, the double commutant of the represented local algebra. Recall that the commutant is defined for any subalgebra ℬ{\mathcal{B}} of the bounded operators ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}) on Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} by

ℬ′={A∈ℬ⁡(ℋ):[A,B]=0​∀B∈ℬ}.{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}=\{A\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}):[A,B]=0~\forall B\in{\mathcal{B}}\}.

A basic result asserts that the algebra 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) is also the closure of πω​(𝒜​(𝒪))\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) in the weak topology of ℋω{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega} – as such, and because it contains the unit operator and is stable under the adjoint, 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) is a (concrete) von Neumann algebra.

Exercise 29.

Show that for any subalgebra ℬ{\mathcal{B}} of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}) one has ℬ⊂ℬ′′{\mathcal{B}}\subset{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime\prime} and ℬ′′′=ℬ′{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime\prime\prime}={\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}. Therefore 𝔐ω​(𝒪)′′=𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}).

There is a good rationale for this construction. The norm topology of the C∗C^{*}-algebra (which coincides with the norm topology ℬ⁡(ℋω){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{\omega}) in a faithful representation) is quite stringent: we have already seen that there are no nonconstant continuous curves in the Weyl algebra. For example, a Weyl generator differs from all its nontrivial translates by operators of norm 22. The situation is different in the weak topology: if translations are implemented in a strongly continuous way then matrix elements of an observable change continuously as the observable is translated. This motivates the weak topology as a better measure of proximity than the norm topology. Note also that Einstein causality implies that the commutant πω​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime} contains all local algebras πω​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})) where 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is causally disjoint from 𝒪\mathcal{O}. As πω​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′=πω​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′′=𝔐ω​(𝒪)′\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime}=\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime}, we see that also 𝔐ω​(𝒪1)⊂𝔐ω​(𝒪)′{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\subset{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime}. It is natural to interpret 𝔐ω​(𝒪)′{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime} in terms of (limits of) observables localised in the causal complement of 𝒪\mathcal{O} and further natural to assume that there are no nontrivial observables that can be localised both in 𝒪\mathcal{O} and its causal complement. This motivates an assumption that

𝔐ω​(𝒪)∩𝔐ω​(𝒪)′=ℂ​𝟙,{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})\cap{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime}=\mathbb{C}{\mathbb{1}},

that is, that the local algebras are factors, so called because an equivalent statement is that

𝔐ω​(𝒪)∨𝔐ω​(𝒪)′=ℬ⁡(ℋ),{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})\vee{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime}={\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}),

i.e., 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) and its commutant generate [in the sense of von Neumann algebras] the full algebra of bounded operators on ℋ{\mathcal{H}}.

The connection to von Neumann algebras permits a vast body of technical work to be brought to bear on AQFT, and indeed some of it was spurred by developments in AQFT. One of the most striking examples is the 1985 result of Fredenhagen [Fre85] that for physically reasonably states ω\omega of reasonable theories obeying the AQFT axioms, every 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) is a type III1 factor. Shortly afterwards, Haagerup [Haa87] proved that there was a unique hyperfinite type III1 factor. A further paper of Buchholz, D’Antoni and Fredenhagen [BDF87] pointed out the local algebras of QFT are hyperfinite, therefore fixing them uniquely up to isomorphism. Remarkably, the local algebras themselves are completely independent of the theory! Therefore the distinction between different theories lies purely in the ‘relative position’ of the local algebras within the bounded operators on Hilbert space.

To appreciate these results and their consequences, we need to delve into the classification of von Neumann factors. Type I factors are easily defined and familiar.

Definition 30.

A von Neumann factor 𝔐{\mathfrak{M}} on Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is of type I if there is a unitary U:ℋ→ℋ1⊗ℋ2U:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}_{2}, for some Hilbert spaces ℋi{\mathcal{H}}_{i}, so that 𝔐=U∗​(ℬ⁡(ℋ1)⊗𝟙ℋ2)​U{\mathfrak{M}}=U^{*}({\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{1})\otimes{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{2}})U. The type is further classified according to the dimension of ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1}.

One could say that type I factors are the natural playground of quantum mechanics: in an obvious way, they are the observables of one party in a bipartite system. The result mentioned above indicates that QFT prefers type III for its local algebras.

Definition 31.

A von Neumann factor 𝔐{\mathfrak{M}} on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is of type III if every nonzero projection E∈𝔐E\in{\mathfrak{M}} may be written in the form

E=W​W∗,for some W∈𝔐 obeying W∗​W=𝟙ℋ.E=WW^{*},\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for some $W\in{\mathfrak{M}}$ obeying $W^{*}W={\mathbb{1}}_{\mathcal{H}}$.}

(It is then the case that every two projections EE and FF in 𝔐{\mathfrak{M}} can be written as E=W​W∗E=WW^{*}, F=W∗​WF=W^{*}W for some W∈𝔐W\in{\mathfrak{M}}.)

Type III1 is a further subtype whose definition would take us too far afield, but it should already be clear that types I and III are quite different. The foregoing definitions are quite technical in nature. However the proof that the local algebras have type III is founded on physical principles, namely that (a) the theory should have a description in terms of quantum fields, (b) that the nn-point functions of these fields have a well-behaved scaling limit at short distances and (c) that there are no local observables localised at a point, other than multiples of the unit. In more detail, the assumptions are:

  1. (a)

    There is a dense domain 𝒟⊂ℋω{\mathscr{D}}\subset{\mathcal{H}}_{\omega} and a linear map ϕ\phi from real-valued test functions to symmetric operators f↦ϕ⁡(f)f\mapsto\phi(f) defined on 𝒟{\mathscr{D}} and obeying ϕ⁡(f)​𝒟⊂𝒟\phi(f){\mathscr{D}}\subset{\mathscr{D}}, so that ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f) has a closure affiliated1212 12 That is, in the polar decomposition ϕ⁡(f)¯=U​|ϕ⁡(f)¯|\overline{\phi(f)}=U|\overline{\phi(f)}| of the closure ϕ⁡(f)¯\overline{\phi(f)} of ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f), the operator UU and any bounded function of |ϕ⁡(f)¯||\overline{\phi(f)}| belong to 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}). to 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) for any 𝒪\mathcal{O} containing supp⁡f\supp f. Furthermore, the nn-point functions of the fields ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f) define distributions

    Wn(f1,…,fn)=⟨Ωω|ϕ(f1)⋯ϕ(fn)Ωω⟩.W_{n}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})=\langle\Omega_{\omega}|\phi(f_{1})\cdots\phi(f_{n})\Omega_{\omega}\rangle.
  2. (b)

    Defining scaling maps on test functions by (βp,λ​f)​(x)=f⁡((x−p)/λ)(\beta_{p,\lambda}f)(x)=f((x-p)/\lambda), there should be a positive monotone function ν\nu so that the scaling limit nn-point functions

    Wns.l.​(f1,…,fn)=limλ→0+ν​(λ)n​Wn​(βp,λ​f1,…,βp,λ​fn)W_{n}^{\text{s.l.}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})=\lim_{\lambda\to 0^{+}}\nu(\lambda)^{n}W_{n}(\beta_{p,\lambda}f_{1},\ldots,\beta_{p,\lambda}f_{n})

    exist and satisfy the (vacuum) Wightman axioms [SW00]. One may think of this theory as living in the tangent space at pp; it is not usually the same theory as the one we started with.

  3. (c)

    It is required that ⋂𝒪∋p𝔐ω​(𝒪)=ℂ​𝟙\bigcap_{\mathcal{O}\owns p}{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})=\mathbb{C}{\mathbb{1}}, where the intersection is taken over all local regions containing the point pp.

Assuming condition (a), we say that ω\omega has a regular scaling limit at p∈𝕄p\in\mathbb{M} if the conditions (b) and (c) hold. Fredenhagen’s result [Fre85] can now be stated precisely.

Theorem 32.

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be a double-cone. If the state ω\omega has a regular scaling limit at some point of the spacelike boundary of 𝒪\mathcal{O} (i.e., its equatorial sphere) then 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) has type III1.

Conversely, if any local von Neumann algebra of a double-cone has type other than III1, then at least one of the assumptions (b),(c) must fail at every point on its spacelike boundary, or (a) fails. One application of this argument has been to prove that ‘SJ states’ of the free field on double-cone regions do not extend to Hadamard states on a larger region - typically because the stress-energy tensor diverges as the boundary is approached [FV13]. We will say a little more about this below.

Various key distinctions between quantum mechanics and QFT can be attributed to the differences between factors of types I and III, and the fact that the local algebras of QFT are typically type III. To conclude this section, we collect some properties of type III factors and their consequences for QFT, gathered under some catchy slogans. We assume that the Hilbert space on which the type III factors act is infinite-dimensional and separable.

All eigenvalues have infinite degeneracy

No type III factor can contain a finite-rank projection; for if EE is finite rank, then writing E=W​W∗E=WW^{*} for an isometry WW, we see that W∗​E​W=W∗​W​W∗​W=𝟙ℋW^{*}EW=W^{*}WW^{*}W={\mathbb{1}}_{\mathcal{H}} is also finite rank, contradicting our assumption on the dimension of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. It follows that no self-adjoint element of a local algebra 𝔐⁡(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}) can have a finite-dimensional eigenspace, which is far removed from the situation of elementary textbook quantum mechanics. In particular, if Ω\Omega is the vacuum vector, then the projection |Ω⟩​⟨Ω||\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega| belongs to no local algebra 𝔐⁡(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}), nor to any commutant 𝔐ω​(𝒪)′{\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime} [because the commutant of a type III factor is also of type III].

Local states are impure

Any state ω\omega on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) restricts in a natural way to a state ω|𝒜⁡(𝒪)\omega|_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})} on each local algebra 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}). What sort of state is it? To start, we note the simple:

Lemma 33.

Suppose ω\omega is a pure state on a C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Then the von Neumann algebra 𝔐=πω​(𝒜)′′{\mathfrak{M}}=\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime} in the GNS representation of ω\omega is a type I factor.

Proof.

The GNS representation of a pure state is irreducible. So the commutant πω​(𝒜)′\pi_{\omega}({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime} consists only of multiples of the unit, and 𝔐=ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{M}}={\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}), which is evidently type I. ∎

In the light of this result, it may not be so much of a surprise that:

Theorem 34.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 32, the algebra πω|𝒜⁡(𝒪)​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′\pi_{\omega|_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})}}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime} is of type III. Therefore ω|𝒜⁡(𝒪)\omega|_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})} is not pure, nor is it a normal state in the GNS representation of a pure state of 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}). Furthermore, in the case where 𝔐ω​(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}_{\omega}(\mathcal{O}) is a factor, the previous statements hold if ω\omega is replaced by any state in its folium.

Proof.

This requires a few standard results from von Neumann theory and can be found as Corollary 3.3 in [FV13]. ∎

The SJ states mentioned above induce pure states and therefore it follows that they cannot be induced as restrictions of states on 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) with good scaling limit properties. See [FV13].

Local experiments can be prepared locally

Suppose EE is any projection in 𝔐⁡(𝒪){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}) and let ω\omega be any state on the C∗C^{*}-algebra formed as the closure of ⋃𝒪𝔐⁡(𝒪)\bigcup_{\mathcal{O}}{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}) in ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}). By the type III property, we may write

E=W​W∗E=WW^{*}

for some isometry W∈𝔐⁡(𝒪)W\in{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}). Then the modified state (Exercise: check that it is a state!)

ωW​(A):=ω⁡(W∗​A​W)\omega_{W}(A):=\omega(W^{*}AW)

obeys

ωW​(E)=ω⁡(W∗​W​W∗​W)=1\omega_{W}(E)=\omega(W^{*}WW^{*}W)=1

so the yes/no test represented by EE is certainly passed in state ωW\omega_{W}. On the other hand, if A∈𝔐⁡(𝒪1)A\in{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) where 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is causally disjoint from 𝒪\mathcal{O}, then A∈𝔐​(𝒪)′A\in{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O})^{\prime} and so

ωW​(A)=ω⁡(W∗​A​W)=ω⁡(W∗​W​A)=ω⁡(A).\omega_{W}(A)=\omega(W^{*}AW)=\omega(W^{*}WA)=\omega(A).

So by changing the state in this way we can prepare a state with a desired property in our lab without changing the rest of the world.

For a brief survey of this and other features of type III factors and their relevance to QFT, see [Yng05, Yng15].

7 The split property

The fundamental postulates of relativistic physics entail that two spacelike separated laboratories should not be able to communicate. Consequently, an experimenter situated in one of these laboratories should be able to conduct experiments independently of the actions (or even the presence) of an experimenter in the other region. The Einstein causality condition A3 reflects this idea, because any observable from one local algebra will commute, and be simultaneously measurable, with any observable from the other. However, this is far from being the only way in which the two regions must be independent. For example, the two observers should be able to prepare their experiments for measurement independently, too. In quantum mechanics this independence is modelled by assigning each of the two local systems their own Hilbert space, ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} and ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2}, on which the observables in the two laboratories respectively act. If the experimenters prepare states ψi\psi_{i}, the global state is then taken to be ψ1⊗ψ2\psi_{1}\otimes\psi_{2} on the tensor product ℋ1⊗ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}_{2}. This section describes the split property which provides conditions under which a similar level of independence may be established in QFT.

First, we introduce some terminology: two von Neumann algebras 𝔐1{\mathfrak{M}}_{1} and 𝔐2{\mathfrak{M}}_{2} acting on a Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} are said to form a split inclusion if there is a type I von Neumann factor 𝔑{\mathfrak{N}} so that

𝔐1⊂𝔑⊂𝔐2.{\mathfrak{M}}_{1}\subset{\mathfrak{N}}\subset{\mathfrak{M}}_{2}.

By Definition 30, this means that there is a unitary U:ℋ→ℋ1⊗ℋ2U:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}_{2} with 𝔑=U∗​(ℬ⁡(ℋ1)⊗𝟙ℋ2)​U{\mathfrak{N}}=U^{*}({\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{1})\otimes{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{2}})U for some Hilbert spaces ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} and ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2}. The commutant of 𝔑{\mathfrak{N}} is easily described:

𝔑′=U∗​(𝟙ℋ1⊗ℬ⁡(ℋ2))​U{\mathfrak{N}}^{\prime}=U^{*}({\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{1}}\otimes{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{2}))U

and it follows from the split inclusion that

𝔐1⊂U∗​(ℬ⁡(ℋ1)⊗𝟙ℋ2)​U,𝔐2′⊂U∗​(𝟙ℋ1⊗ℬ⁡(ℋ2))​U.{\mathfrak{M}}_{1}\subset U^{*}({\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{1})\otimes{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{2}})U,\hskip 20.00003pt{\mathfrak{M}}_{2}^{\prime}\subset U^{*}({\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{1}}\otimes{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{2}))U.

Suppose that states ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2} are given on 𝔐1{\mathfrak{M}}_{1} and 𝔐2′{\mathfrak{M}}_{2}^{\prime} that may be expressed in terms of density matrices ρi\rho_{i} on ℋi{\mathcal{H}}_{i}, so that

ω1​(A)=tr⁡((ρ1⊗𝟙ℋ2)​U​A​U∗),ω2​(B)=tr⁡((𝟙ℋ1⊗ρ2)​U​B​U∗)\omega_{1}(A)=\tr((\rho_{1}\otimes{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{2}})UAU^{*}),\hskip 20.00003pt\omega_{2}(B)=\tr(({\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{1}}\otimes\rho_{2})UBU^{*})

for A∈𝔐1A\in{\mathfrak{M}}_{1}, B∈𝔐2′B\in{\mathfrak{M}}_{2}^{\prime}. Then there is an obvious joint state

ω⁡(C)=tr⁡((ρ1⊗ρ2)​U​A​U∗)\omega(C)=\tr((\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2})UAU^{*})

with the property (Exercise: prove it!) that

ω⁡(A​B)=ω1​(A)​ω2​(B)=ω⁡(B​A),for all​A∈𝔐1,B∈𝔐2′.\omega(AB)=\omega_{1}(A)\omega_{2}(B)=\omega(BA),\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for all}~A\in{\mathfrak{M}}_{1},~B\in{\mathfrak{M}}_{2}^{\prime}.

With a little more technical work it can be shown that this construction is possible whenever ωi\omega_{i} are given as density matrices on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} (see e.g., [Few16] for an exposition).

Returning to QFT, we make the following definition.

Definition 35.

A net 𝒪↦𝔐⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{O}\mapsto{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}) of von Neumann algebras has the split property if, whenever 𝒪1¯⊂𝒪2\overline{\mathcal{O}_{1}}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}, the inclusion 𝔐⁡(𝒪1)⊂𝔐⁡(𝒪2){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\subset{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) is a split inclusion.

Note that we only require a split inclusion when 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} contains the closure of 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}, so that there is a ‘safety margin’ or collar around 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} within 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. We can also make the less restrictive assumption that the split inclusion holds when this safety margin has a minimum size, in which case one speaks of the distal split property.

If the split property holds, and 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3} are spacelike separated pre-compact regions whose closures do not intersect, then we may certainly find a pre-compact neighbourhood 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} of 𝒪¯1\overline{\mathcal{O}}_{1} within the causal complement of 𝒪3¯\overline{\mathcal{O}_{3}}. Then 𝔐⁡(𝒪1)⊂𝔐⁡(𝒪2){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\subset{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) is split and 𝔐⁡(𝒪3)⊂𝔐​(𝒪2)′{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{3})\subset{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{2})^{\prime}. It follows that experimenters in 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{3} are able to independently prepare and measure observables of the field theory. Moreover, there is an isomorphism of von Neumann algebras

𝔐⁡(𝒪1)​⊗¯​𝔐​(𝒪3)≅𝔐⁡(𝒪1)∨𝔐⁡(𝒪3){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\bar{\otimes}{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{3})\cong{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\vee{\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{3})

extending the map A⊗B↦A​BA\otimes B\mapsto AB, where the left-hand side is a spatial tensor product of von Neumann algebras and the right-hand side is the von Neumann algebra generated by sums and products of elements in 𝔐⁡(𝒪1){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) and 𝔐⁡(𝒪3){\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{3}).

In situations where the Reeh–Schlieder theorem applies, and there is a vector that is cyclic and separating for all causally convex bounded regions, the split inclusions have more structure and are called standard split inclusions. A deep analysis by Doplicher and Longo [DL84] shows, among many other things, that there is a canonical choice for the type I factor appearing in standard split inclusions.

The split property is enjoyed by free scalar fields of mass m≥0m\geq 0 and the observable algebra for the Dirac field, but also for certain interacting models in 1+11+1-dimensions (see [Lec15] for a survey and exposition). It is intimately connected to the way in which the number of local degrees of freedom available to the theory grows with the energy scale. These are expressed technically in terms of various nuclearity conditions, which we will not describe in detail here (but see [Few16] for discussion and a relation to yet a further topic – Quantum Energy Inequalities). Instead, we limit ourselves to some examples involving a theory comprising countably many independent free scalar fields of masses mrm_{r} (r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}). It may be shown, for instance, that this theory has the split property if the function

G(β):=∑r=1∞e−βmr/4G(\beta):=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}e^{-\beta m_{r}/4}

is finite for all β>0\beta>0 and grows at most polynomially in β−1\beta^{-1} as β→0+\beta\to 0^{+}. This is the case if mr=r​m1m_{r}=rm_{1}, for instance. On the other hand, if

mr=(2​d0)−1​log⁡(r+1)m_{r}=(2d_{0})^{-1}\log(r+1)

for some constant d0>0d_{0}>0 then the series defining G⁡(β)G(\beta) diverges for β≤8​d0\beta\leq 8d_{0}. Further analysis [DDFL87, Thm 4.3] shows that the split property fails in this situation, but that the distal split condition holds provided that the ‘safety margin’ is sufficiently large. For concentric arrangements of double cones of base radii rr and r+dr+d, splitting fails if d<d0d<d_{0} and succeeds if d>2​d0d>2d_{0}.

The overall message is that a (well-behaved) tensor product structure across regions at spacelike separation can only be expected in well-behaved QFTs and with a safety margin between the regions. It turns out that the split property is closely related both to the existence of well-behaved thermal states (absence of a Hagedorn temperature) and to whether the theory satisfies quantum energy inequalities – see [Few16] for discussion and original references. Intuitively, the reason for this is that there is a cost associated with disentangling the degrees of freedom between the two regions. For example, a joint state ‘glued together’ from two states given on their local algebras might be expected to have a higher energy than the sum of the two original energies, with the excess in energy being higher if the ‘gluing’ has to take place over a smaller gap between the regions. If the number of degrees of freedom available grows excessively with the energy scale, it becomes impossible to achieve the gluing with a finite excess energy, or possible only if the regions are sufficiently distant from one another.

8 Superselection sectors

We come back to the discussion of superselection sectors, mentioned in section 2.1. In the algebraic viewpoint on quantum theory, superselection sectors correspond to a class of unitarily inequivalent representations of the algebra of observables. One of the major structural results in algebraic quantum field theory [DHR69a, DHR69b, DHR71, DHR74, DR89] was to show that these sectors are related to irreducible representations of some compact Lie group GG (the global gauge group). The key idea of algebraic QFT is that all the relevant information is contained in the net of observables, and from this net one can construct an algebra of fields ℱ⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}), which then contains non-observable objects, e.g. smeared Dirac fields ψ⁡(f)\psi(f) (see section 4.2). This algebra is uniquely fixed by the net and it carries the action of the gauge group GG, so that local algebra 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) consists of elements of ℱ⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{O}) invariant under GG. The reconstruction of both ℱ{\mathcal{F}} and GG is achieved through the DHR (Doplicher–Haag–Roberts) analysis [DHR69a, DHR69b, DHR71, DHR74] together with the Doplicher–Roberts reconstruction theorem [DR89]. The brief exposition in Sections 8.1-8.3 is based on [Fre95].

As motivating example, we consider the complex scalar field, whose algebra 𝒞⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{M}) was described in Sec. 4.2. Its vacuum representation π\pi is given by

π⁡(Φ⁡(g))\displaystyle\pi(\Phi(g)) =a⁡(g^|Hm+)⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗a∗​(g^|Hm+)\displaystyle=a(\hat{g}|_{H_{m}^{+}})\otimes{\mathbb{1}}+{\mathbb{1}}\otimes a^{*}(\hat{g}|_{H_{m}^{+}})
π​(Φ⋆​(g))\displaystyle\pi(\Phi^{\star}(g)) =a∗​(g^|Hm+)⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗a⁡(g^|Hm+)\displaystyle=a^{*}(\hat{g}|_{H_{m}^{+}})\otimes{\mathbb{1}}+{\mathbb{1}}\otimes a(\hat{g}|_{H_{m}^{+}})

for real-valued gg [with Φ⁡(g)=Φ⁡(Re⁡g)+i​Φ​(Im⁡g)\Phi(g)=\Phi(\Re g)+i\Phi(\Im g) in general, compare with the real scalar field in Section 4.3], on 𝔉⁡(ℋ)⊗𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H})\otimes{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H}), where ℋ=L2​(Hm+,d​μ)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(H^{+}_{m},d\mu) and a∗,aa^{*},a are creation and annihilation operators on the Fock space 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H}). The charge operator is

Q=N⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗N,Q=N\otimes{\mathbb{1}}-{\mathbb{1}}\otimes N\,,

where NN is the number operator on 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H}) (see Appendix C for definition). The theory has a global U⁡(1)U(1) gauge symmetry generated by QQ:

ei​α​Q​π​(Φ⁡(f))​e−i​α​Q=e−i​α​π​(Φ⁡(f)),α∈ℝ,e^{i\alpha Q}\pi(\Phi(f))e^{-i\alpha Q}=e^{-i\alpha}\pi(\Phi(f)),\hskip 20.00003pt\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, (45)

which implements the automorphisms ηα\eta_{\alpha} described earlier, and the Fock space decomposes into charged sectors

𝔉⁡(ℋ)⊗𝔉⁡(ℋ)=⨁q∈ℤℋq,{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H})\otimes\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H})=\bigoplus_{q\in\mathbb{Z}}{\mathcal{H}}_{q},

each ℋq{\mathcal{H}}_{q} being the eigenspace of QQ with eigenvalue qq. Assuming that QQ is conserved in all interactions available to the observer, the argument described in Sec. 2.1 shows that the observables of the theory should commute with QQ and be block-diagonal in this decomposition. Clearly, this is not the case for the smeared fields π⁡(Φ⁡(f))\pi(\Phi(f)) or π​(Φ⋆​(f))\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f)), which are consequently unobservable. On the other hand, operators of the form π​(Φ⋆​(f)​Φ​(f))\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f)\Phi(f)) is gauge-invariant, as is (any smearing of) the Wick product of the field π​(Φ⋆​(x))\pi(\Phi^{\star}(x)) with π⁡(Φ⁡(x))\pi(\Phi(x)).

The main point of interest for us is that the local observable algebras 𝒞obs​(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O}) are gauge-invariant by definition and therefore π​(𝒞obs​(𝒪))\pi({\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O})) consists of block-diagonal operators. More than that, we can see that there are representations πq\pi_{q} of 𝒞obs​(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O}) on each ℋq{\mathcal{H}}_{q}, given by

πq​(A)=Pq​π​(A)​Pq,\pi_{q}(A)=P_{q}\pi(A)P_{q},

where PqP_{q} is the orthogonal projector onto ℋq{\mathcal{H}}_{q} within 𝔉⁡(ℋ)⊗𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H})\otimes{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H}). In particular, π0\pi_{0} is a representation in ℋ0{\mathcal{H}}_{0}, the charge-zero sector, which contains the vacuum vector Ω⊗Ω∈𝔉⁡(ℋ)⊗𝔉⁡(ℋ)\Omega\otimes\Omega\in{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H})\otimes{\mathfrak{F}}(\mathcal{H}) and will be called the vacuum sector for the observables.

We now have a whole family of representations of the algebras 𝒞obs​(𝒪){\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O}) on different Hilbert spaces. It is easy to argue (at least heuristically) that these are mutually unitarily inequivalent, because the charge operator itself can be regarded as a limit of local observables, i.e., local integrals of the Noether charge density associated with the global gauge symmetry. Therefore, if there were a unitary U:ℋq→ℋq′U:{\mathcal{H}}_{q}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{q^{\prime}} obeying πq′​(A)=U​πq​(A)​U−1\pi_{q}^{\prime}(A)=U\pi_{q}(A)U^{-1} for all A∈𝒞obs​(𝒪)A\in{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{obs}}(\mathcal{O}) and all local regions 𝒪\mathcal{O}, it would follow that the charge operators in the two representations should be equivalent under the same mapping, giving

q′​𝟙ℋq′=q​U​𝟙ℋq​U−1=q​𝟙ℋq′q^{\prime}{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{q^{\prime}}}=qU{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{q}}U^{-1}=q{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{q^{\prime}}}

which can only happen in the case q′=qq^{\prime}=q. The physical distinction between different sectors is precisely that they have different charge content, and the central insight of the DHR programme is that the relevant charges might be gathered in some local region, outside which the distinction can be, as it were, gauged away. An extra charged particle behind the moon ought not to change our description of particle physics on earth.1313 13 This picturesque statement applies to confined charges rather than those with long range interactions such as electric charges. We discuss this issue briefly later on. As we will describe this physical insight allows a remarkable reversal of the process we have just followed: instead of starting with an algebra of unobservable fields transforming under a global gauge group and obtaining from it a collection of unitarily inequivalent representations of the algebra of observables, one starts from a suitable class of representations of the observable algebras and attempts to reconstruct the unobservable fields and the a unifying gauge group.

8.1 Representations of interest in particle physics

In the first step of DHR analysis we want to single out a class of representations relevant for study of superselection sectors. We focus on theories without long range effects, for example strong interactions in hadron physics. Loosely speaking, the representations of interest correspond to states that are generated from the vacuum by (possibly unobservable) local field operators. The intuition is that these states have different global charges (e.g. QCD charges) but which are localized in compact regions.

Let 𝒪↦𝒜⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{O}\mapsto{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) be a net of C∗C^{*}-algebras and let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be the quasilocal algebra (to reduce clutter, we write 𝒜⁡(𝕄)≡𝒜{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})\equiv{\mathcal{A}} in this section). Let π0\pi_{0} be the vacuum representation (assumed here to be faithful).

We are interested in reconstructing the field algebras ℱ⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}) realized as von Neumann algebras of operators on some common Hilbert space ℋt​o​t\mathcal{H}_{tot}, i.e. ℱ⁡(𝒪)⊂ℬ⁡(ℋt​o​t)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O})\subset\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{tot}). We want them to satisfy (among others) the following properties:

  1. F1

    ℱ⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}) carries a strongly continuous representation of the (covering group) of the Poincaré group and there exists a unique vector Ω∈ℋt​o​t\Omega\in\mathcal{H}_{tot} (up to phase) that is invariant under this action.

  2. F2

    There exists a compact group GG (the gauge group) and a strongly continuous faithful representation UU of GG in ℋt​o​t\mathcal{H}_{tot} such that the automorphism A↦αg​(A)=AdU⁡(g)​(A)=U⁡(g)​A​U​(g)−1A\mapsto\alpha_{g}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U(g)}(A)=U(g)AU(g)^{-1} obeys

    αg​(ℱ⁡(𝒪))=ℱ⁡(𝒪),U⁡(g)​Ω=Ω,\alpha_{g}(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}))=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O})\,,\hskip 20.00003ptU(g)\Omega=\Omega\,,

    and the U⁡(g)U(g)’s commute with the representation of the Poincaré group mentioned above.

    On general grounds, the Hilbert space ℋt​o​t\mathcal{H}_{tot} decomposes into superselection sectors as:

    ℋt​o​t=⨁σℋ~σ⊗ℋσ,U⁡(g)=⨁σUσ​(g)⊗𝟙ℋσ,\mathcal{H}_{tot}=\bigoplus_{\sigma}\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}\,,\hskip 20.00003ptU(g)=\bigoplus_{\sigma}U_{\sigma}(g)\otimes{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}}\,, (46)

    where the sum is taken over equivalence classes σ\sigma of unitary irreps (ℋ~σ,Uσ)(\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma},U_{\sigma}) of GG, with representation space ℋ~σ\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} and ℋσ\mathcal{H}_{\sigma} reflects the multiplicity with which these representations appear (including the possibility that ℋσ\mathcal{H}_{\sigma} has zero dimension, in which case σ\sigma does not appear).

  3. F3

    Reconstructing the observables: ℋt​o​t\mathcal{H}_{tot} carries a representation π\pi of 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) and

    π(𝒜(𝒪))′′=ℱ(𝒪)∩U(G)′={A∈ℱ(𝒪),αg(A)=A,∀g∈G}.\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime}={\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{O})\cap U(G)^{\prime}=\{A\in\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}),\alpha_{g}(A)=A,\forall g\in G\}.

    By construction, this representation decomposes w.r.t.  (46) as

    π=⨁σ𝟙ℋ~σ⊗πσ\pi=\bigoplus_{\sigma}{\mathbb{1}}_{\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}}\otimes\pi_{\sigma}

    where each πσ\pi_{\sigma} is a representation of 𝒜⁡(𝒪){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) on ℋσ\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}. In particular, the representation corresponding to the trivial representation of GG should coincide with π0\pi_{0}, the vacuum representation.

The task of reconstructing the field algebra therefore amounts to determining the relevant representations πσ\pi_{\sigma}, and corresponding (irreducible) representations UσU_{\sigma} of GG, which can then be assembled to form ℋt​o​t\mathcal{H}_{tot}. It may be shown that the representations πσ\pi_{\sigma} of interest are those which satisfy the following criterion (due to DHR [DHR71]):

Definition 36.

A representation π\pi of a net of C∗C^{*}-algebras 𝒪↦𝒜⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{O}\mapsto{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) is a DHR representation if it is Poincaré covariant and the following holds:

π|𝒜⁡(𝒪′)≅π0|𝒜⁡(𝒪′)\pi\big|_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime})}\cong\pi_{0}\big|_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime})} (47)

for all double-cones1414 14 The criterion can be weakened so as to refer to sufficiently large double-cones. 𝒪\mathcal{O}, where 𝒪′\mathcal{O}^{\prime} is the causal complement of 𝒪\mathcal{O} and ≅\cong means unitary equivalence, i.e. there exists a unitary operator between the appropriate Hilbert spaces V:ℋ0→ℋπV:\mathcal{H}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{\pi} such that V​π0​(A)=π⁡(A)​VV\pi_{0}(A)=\pi(A)V for all A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪′)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}).

In the above definition, the region 𝒪′\mathcal{O}^{\prime} is unbounded, so 𝒜⁡(𝒪′){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}) is not given a priori in the specification of the theory. It is defined to be the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by all local algebras 𝒜⁡(𝒪1){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) for bounded 𝒪1⊂𝒪′\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}^{\prime}.

The intertwining unitary VV has the interpretation of a charge-carrying field. To get some intuition about these objects, consider the example of a complex scalar field mentioned at the beginning of this section. Consider a test function f∈C0∞​(𝕄,ℝ)f\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M};\mathbb{R}) with Φ⋆​(f)≠0\Phi^{\star}(f)\neq 0. Firstly, we note that the charge is related to the phase of the field π​(Φ⋆​(f))\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f)), so in order to extract an intertwiner VV, we consider the polar decomposition π​(Φ⋆​(f))¯=Vf​|π​(Φ⋆​(f))¯|\overline{\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f))}=V_{f}|\overline{\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f))}|, where the overline denotes an operator closure. The partial isometry VfV_{f} may be taken to be unitary because π​(Φ⋆​(f))¯\overline{\pi(\Phi^{\star}(f))} is normal; acting on vectors in the vacuum sector ℋ0{\mathcal{H}}_{0}, it has the property Vfq​π0​(A)=πq​(A)​VfqV_{f}^{q}\pi_{0}(A)=\pi_{q}(A)V_{f}^{q}, where A∈𝒞⁡(𝕄)A\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{M}) and πq\pi_{q} is the representation with charge q∈ℤq\in\mathbb{Z}. We see that VfV_{f} creates a single unit of charge and the support of ff determines the region, where the charge is localized. If ff is supported in a double cone 𝒪\mathcal{O} and we take f1f_{1} supported inside another double cone 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}, then Vf1q​Vf−qV_{f_{1}}^{q}V_{f}^{-q} transports qq units of charge from 𝒪\mathcal{O} to 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}.

There exists a generalization of the DHR framework to the situation, where charges are not localized in bounded regions, but rather in cone-like regions (space-like cones formed as a causal completions of spacial cones). This is relevant if one wants to apply this analysis to theories with long-range interactions, e.g. quantum electrodynamics (QED). It is expected that the electron is a charged particle with this type of localization. The corresponding version of the DHR construction has been developed by Buchholz and Fredenhagen (BF analysis) in [BF82] and the full analysis of superselection sectors for QED has been achieved in [BR14].

We may now turn things around and phrase our problem as follows: starting with the abstract algebra of observables and its vacuum representation we want to classify the equivalence classes of its (irreducible) representations satisfying (47). Following the literature [Haa96, DHR69a, DHR69b, DHR71, DHR74], we call each of these equivalence classes a superselection sector (also called charge superselection sectors, whereupon the labels σ\sigma are referred to as charges, though they need not be numbers).

A special case is the situation where (Uσ,ℋ~σ)(U_{\sigma},\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}) is a one-dimensional representation. Remarkably, such simple sectors are distinguished by the following property of πσ\pi_{\sigma}:

Definition 37.

We say that a representation π\pi satisfies Haag duality, if

π​(𝒜⁡(𝒪′))′′=π​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′∩π​(𝒜)′′,\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}))^{\prime\prime}=\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime}\cap\pi({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime}\,, (48)

for any double-cone 𝒪\mathcal{O}. If π\pi is irreducible then the intersection with π​(𝒜)′′\pi({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime} is superfluous, whereupon one also has

π​(𝒜⁡(𝒪′))′=π​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′.\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}))^{\prime}=\pi({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime}\,. (49)

(Exercise!)

One can show that πσ\pi_{\sigma} satisfies Haag duality if and only if ℋ~σ\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} is one-dimensional [DHR69a]. In particular, the vacuum sector is always simple; however, if the global gauge group is nonabelian, there will necessarily be some non-simple sectors.

Exercise 38.

If 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a C∗C^{*}-algebra with Hilbert space representations π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} on Hilbert spaces ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} and ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2}, define the representation (π1⊕π2)​(A)=π1​(A)⊕π2​(A)(\pi_{1}\oplus\pi_{2})(A)=\pi_{1}(A)\oplus\pi_{2}(A) on ℋ1⊕ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\oplus{\mathcal{H}}_{2}. Compute the commutant (π1⊕π2)​(𝒜)′(\pi_{1}\oplus\pi_{2})({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime} and double commutant (π1⊕π2)​(𝒜)′′(\pi_{1}\oplus\pi_{2})({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime} within ℬ⁡(ℋ1⊕ℋ2){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{H}}_{1}\oplus{\mathcal{H}}_{2}), which may be regarded as consisting of 2×22\times 2 ‘block matrices’ of operators, and compare the results with π1​(𝒜)′′⊕π2​(𝒜)′′\pi_{1}({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime}\oplus\pi_{2}({\mathcal{A}})^{\prime\prime}.

8.2 Localized endomorphisms

We now want to introduce some algebraic structures on the space of representations of interest, following closely the exposition presented in [Fre95]. Our standing assumptions are that the vacuum representation π0\pi_{0} is faithful and irreducible, satisfies Haag duality, and that the local algebras π0​(𝒜​(𝒪))\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) are weakly closed, π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′=π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime}=\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})), so they are actually von Neumann algebras.1515 15 If weak closure does not hold, one can apply this discussion to the net O↦𝔐0​(𝒪):=π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))′′O\mapsto{\mathfrak{M}}_{0}(\mathcal{O}):=\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))^{\prime\prime}. Together with Haag duality, this gives

π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪′))′=π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪))\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}))^{\prime}=\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O})) (50)

for every double-cone 𝒪\mathcal{O}.

Let us fix a double cone 𝒪\mathcal{O}. Consider a representation π\pi of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} satisfying the DHR criterion with a unitary V:ℋ0→ℋπV:\mathcal{H}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{\pi} implementing the equivalence in (47) for 𝒪\mathcal{O}, and define a representation π~\tilde{\pi} on ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} by

π~​(A)=V−1​π​(A)​V,A∈𝒜.\tilde{\pi}(A)=V^{-1}\pi(A)V\,,\hskip 10.00002ptA\in{\mathcal{A}}\,.

Take 𝒪1⊃𝒪\mathcal{O}_{1}\supset\mathcal{O} and A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪1)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}), B∈𝒜⁡(𝒪1′)B\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}). Since 𝒜⁡(𝒪1′)⊂𝒜⁡(𝒪′){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1})\subset{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}) and π~=π0\tilde{\pi}=\pi_{0} on 𝒜⁡(𝒪′){\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}) (by the DHR criterion), we have

[π0​(B),π~​(A)]=π~​([B,A])=0,[\pi_{0}(B),\tilde{\pi}(A)]=\tilde{\pi}([B,A])=0\,,

so π~​(A)∈π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1′))′=π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))\tilde{\pi}(A)\in\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}))^{\prime}=\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})), where the last assertion follows from Haag duality (50). We conclude that π~​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))⊂π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))\tilde{\pi}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}))\subset\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})), so π~​(𝒜)⊂π0​(𝒜)\tilde{\pi}({\mathcal{A}})\subset\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}), as local operators are dense in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Since π0\pi_{0} is faithful, there exists an endomorphism ρ\rho of the abstract C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} with ρ=π0−1∘π~\rho=\pi_{0}^{-1}\circ\tilde{\pi}.

There is an obvious equivalence relation on endomorphisms:

ρ1∼ρ2⇔ρ1=ι∘ρ2,\rho_{1}\sim\rho_{2}\Leftrightarrow\rho_{1}=\iota\circ\rho_{2}\,, (51)

for some inner automorphism ι\iota, i.e. one that can be written as ι⁡(A)=AdU​(A)=U​A​U−1\iota(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U}(A)=UAU^{-1} for some unitary U∈𝒜U\in{\mathcal{A}}.

Endomorphisms ρ\rho obtained from representations satisfying the DHR criterion for a given 𝒪\mathcal{O} have the following properties: [Fre95]

  1. LE1

    Localised in 𝒪\mathcal{O}: ρ⁡(A)=A\rho(A)=A, A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪′)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}).

  2. LE2

    Transportable: ∀𝒪1,𝒪2\forall\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2} with 𝒪∪𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}\cup\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}, there is a unitary U∈𝒜⁡(𝒪2)U\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) with AdU∘ρ⁡(A)=A\mathrm{Ad}_{U}\circ\rho(A)=A, A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪1′)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}), i.e. for every region 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} there exists an endomorphism equivalent to ρ\rho under (51) that is localized in 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}.

  3. LE3

    ρ⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))⊂𝒜⁡(𝒪1)\rho({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}))\subset{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}), ∀𝒪1⊃𝒪\forall\mathcal{O}_{1}\supset\mathcal{O}. In fact, this is a consequence of LE1 and LE2 by an argument similar to show π~​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))⊂π0​(𝒜⁡(𝒪1))\tilde{\pi}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}))\subset\pi_{0}({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1})) above.

Changing the perspective, we can use the properties above as defining properties for the following class of endomorphisms of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}:

Definition 39.

Given a double-cone 𝒪\mathcal{O}, let Δ⁡(𝒪)\Delta(\mathcal{O}) be the set of all transportable endomorphisms of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} localised in 𝒪\mathcal{O}, i.e. those satisfying LE1 and LE2 (and hence LE3). We define Δ≐⋃𝒪Δ⁡(𝒪)\Delta\doteq\bigcup_{\mathcal{O}}\Delta(\mathcal{O}).

It can be shown that the equivalence classes Δ/∼\Delta/\sim (where ∼\sim is given by (51)) are in one to one correspondence with unitary equivalence classes of representations satisfying (47) (i.e. with superselection sectors). Δ/∼\Delta/\sim is equipped with a natural product (given by the composition of endomorphisms of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}), which induces a product on the space of sectors, namely:

[π1⋅π2]≐[π0∘ρ1​ρ2],[\pi_{1}\cdot\pi_{2}]\doteq[\pi_{0}\circ\rho_{1}\rho_{2}]\,, (52)

where πi≐π0∘ρi\pi_{i}\doteq\pi_{0}\circ\rho_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2.

Exercise 40.

Show that the composition of representations introduced in (52) is well defined and the resulting representation satisfies the DHR criterion.

It can also be shown (see e.g. [Fre95]) that the ⋅\cdot product of two representations that are Poincaré covariant and satisfy the spectrum condition also has these two features. The space of sectors equipped with the composition product is a semigroup with the vacuum sector as the identity. One can verify that simple sectors correspond to morphisms ρ\rho that are in fact automorphisms of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, i.e. ρ⁡(𝒜)=𝒜\rho({\mathcal{A}})={\mathcal{A}}. Hence the space of simple sectors equipped with ⋅\cdot is a group.

Transportability of endomorphisms LE2 is crucial for the DHR analysis, since it allows us to “move morphisms around”. First we establish the following:

Proposition 41.

Endomorphisms ρ\rho are locally commutative, i.e. for 𝒪1⊂𝒪2′\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime} and ρi∈Δ⁡(𝒪i)\rho_{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{O}_{i}) we have ρ1​ρ2=ρ2​ρ1\rho_{1}\rho_{2}=\rho_{2}\rho_{1}.

Proof.

Fix an arbitrary double cone 𝒪\mathcal{O} and choose double cones 𝒪^i\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{i}, 𝒪~i\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 with the following properties: 𝒪^i⊂𝒪′\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{i}\subset\mathcal{O}^{\prime}, 𝒪^i∪𝒪i⊂𝒪~i\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{i}\cup\mathcal{O}_{i}\subset\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 and 𝒪~1⊂𝒪~2′\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{1}\subset\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{2}^{\prime} (see Figure 3).

LE2 implies that there exist unitaries Ui∈𝒜⁡(𝒪~i)U_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{i}) such that AdUi∘ρi=ρ^i∈Δ⁡(𝒪^i)\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{i}}\circ\rho_{i}=\hat{\rho}_{i}\in\Delta(\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2. Hence for any A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) we have ρi​(A)=AdUi∗∘ρ^i​(A)=AdUi∗​(A)\rho_{i}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{i}^{*}}\circ\hat{\rho}_{i}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{i}^{*}}(A), as 𝒪\mathcal{O} is causally disjoint from both 𝒪^1\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{1} and 𝒪^2\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{2} and we have also used LE3. Hence

ρ1​ρ2​(A)=ρ1∘AdU2∗​(A)=Adρ1​(U2∗)∘AdU1∗​(A)=AdU2∗​U1∗​(A)=AdU1∗​U2∗​(A)=ρ2​ρ1​(A),\rho_{1}\rho_{2}(A)=\rho_{1}\circ\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{2}^{*}}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{\rho_{1}(U_{2}^{*})}\circ\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{1}^{*}}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{2}^{*}U_{1}^{*}}(A)=\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{1}^{*}U_{2}^{*}}(A)=\rho_{2}\rho_{1}(A)\,,

where we used LE1 to conclude that ρ1​(U2∗)=U2∗\rho_{1}(U_{2}^{*})=U_{2}^{*}, while U1∗​U2∗=U2∗​U1∗U_{1}^{*}U_{2}^{*}=U_{2}^{*}U_{1}^{*} follows from A3. We can repeat the same reasoning for any double cone 𝒪\mathcal{O}, so ρ1​ρ2=ρ2​ρ1\rho_{1}\rho_{2}=\rho_{2}\rho_{1}. ∎

We can now use this result to show that the product of representations is commutative, i.e. [π1⋅π2]=[π2⋅π1][\pi_{1}\cdot\pi_{2}]=[\pi_{2}\cdot\pi_{1}]. Let ρ1,ρ2∈Δ⁡(𝒪)\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\in\Delta(\mathcal{O}) and take two spacelike separated double cones 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1}, 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. By LE2 there are morphisms ρ~i\tilde{\rho}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 localized in 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} and unitaries UiU_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 such that ρ~i=AdUi∘ρi\tilde{\rho}_{i}=\mathrm{Ad}_{U_{i}}\circ\rho_{i}. It follows by Prop. 41 that

ρ2​ρ1=Adρ2​(U1∗)​U2∗∘ρ~2​ρ~1=Adρ2​(U1∗)​U2∗∘ρ~1​ρ~2=Adε⁡(ρ1,ρ2)∘ρ1​ρ2,\rho_{2}\rho_{1}=\mathrm{Ad}_{\rho_{2}(U_{1}^{*})U_{2}^{*}}\circ\tilde{\rho}_{2}\tilde{\rho}_{1}=\mathrm{Ad}_{\rho_{2}(U_{1}^{*})U_{2}^{*}}\circ\tilde{\rho}_{1}\tilde{\rho}_{2}=\mathrm{Ad}_{\varepsilon(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})}\circ\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\,,

with the unitary

ε⁡(ρ1,ρ2)=ρ2​(U1∗)​U2∗​U1​ρ1​(U2)∈𝒜.\varepsilon(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})=\rho_{2}(U_{1}^{*})U_{2}^{*}U_{1}\rho_{1}(U_{2})\in{\mathcal{A}}\,. (53)

This proves the equivalence of ρ2​ρ1\rho_{2}\rho_{1} and ρ1​ρ2\rho_{1}\rho_{2}, so the commutativity of the product of representations follows. Hence the space of all sectors, equipped with ⋅\cdot is an abelian semigroup and the space of all simple sectors equipped with ⋅\cdot is an abelian group.

The unitary operator ε⁡(ρ1,ρ2)\varepsilon(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}) that we have discovered here is called the statistics operator. It depends only on ρ1\rho_{1}, ρ2\rho_{2} and not on ρ~i\tilde{\rho}_{i} nor the choice of UiU_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2.

Let ερ≡ε⁡(ρ,ρ)\varepsilon_{\rho}\equiv\varepsilon(\rho,\rho). In spacetime dimension d>2d>2 we have ερ2=id\varepsilon_{\rho}^{2}={\textrm{id}}. For simple sectors π0∘ρ2\pi_{0}\circ\rho^{2} is irreducible, so ερ\varepsilon_{\rho} is a multiple of 𝟙\mathds{1} and in d>2d>2 this implies that ερ=±𝟙\varepsilon_{\rho}=\pm\mathds{1}. Physically this corresponds to the alternative between Fermi and Bose statistics. For general sectors in d>2d>2 one can also have para-statistics or even infinite statistics. In lower dimensions (d≤2d\leq 2), ερ\varepsilon_{\rho} is instead related to representations of the braid group. This kind of behaviour appears also for cone-localized charges (BF analysis), but in this case the braided statistics appears already in d≤3d\leq 3. More details relating ερ\varepsilon_{\rho} to statistics will be given in the next section.

The physical interpretation of the product of representations can be understood as follows [DHR71]. Let ω0\omega_{0} be the vacuum state and ρi∈Δ⁡(𝒪i)\rho_{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{O}_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2. We have the two states ωi=ω0∘ρi\omega_{i}=\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{i}, which are vector states in their respective representations π=π0∘ρi\pi=\pi_{0}\circ\rho_{i}; indeed, one suitable vector is the vacuum vector Ω\Omega that is the GNS vector induced by ω0\omega_{0}. Clearly, ω=ω0∘ρ1​ρ2\omega=\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{1}\rho_{2} is a vector state in representation [π1⋅π2][\pi_{1}\cdot\pi_{2}], with the same representing vector. Let 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} be spacelike to 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. Then ω\omega looks like the vector state ω0∘ρ1\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{1} with respect to observations in 𝒪2′\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime} and like ω0∘ρ2\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{2} for observations in 𝒪1′\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}. Hence, taking the product [π1⋅π2][\pi_{1}\cdot\pi_{2}] has a physical interpretation of composing two vector states that are localized “far apart”.

8.3 Intertwiners and permutation symmetry

As stated in the previous section, states ω0∘ρk\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{k}, k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n obtained from transportable localized morphisms ρk∈Δ\rho_{k}\in\Delta are interpreted as vector states corresponding to localized charged particles and composition of morphisms describes creating several such charges in spacetime. Now we want to understand how one may create these charges in a given order. As the state ω0∘ρ1​…​ρn\omega_{0}\circ\rho_{1}\dots\rho_{n} is independent of the ordering of the ρk\rho_{k}’s, this must be done by permuting a family of vectors all of which representing this state. In order to do this, we need some notation.

Definition 42.

Let ρ,σ∈Δ\rho,\sigma\in\Delta. Define the space of intertwiners between ρ\rho and σ\sigma by1616 16 In [DHR71, DHR74] the intertwiners are denoted by 𝐓≡(σ​|T|​ρ)\mathbf{T}\equiv(\sigma|T|\rho), to emphasize to which space they belong.

(σ,ρ)≐{T∈𝒜|σ(A)T=Tρ(A),∀A∈𝒜}.(\sigma,\rho)\doteq\{T\in{\mathcal{A}}|\ \sigma(A)T=T\rho(A),~\forall~A\in{\mathcal{A}}\}\,.

We can now define some algebraic operations on intertwiners. Let S∈(τ,σ)S\in(\tau,\sigma) and T∈(σ,ρ)T\in(\sigma,\rho) be intertwiners. We can compose them to obtain S​T∈(τ,ρ)ST\in(\tau,\rho) and can also define the adjoint T∗∈(ρ,σ)T^{*}\in(\rho,\sigma). Moreover, there is a natural product between intertwiners in different spaces. Let T1∈(σ1,ρ1,)T_{1}\in(\sigma_{1},\rho_{1},) and T2∈(σ2,ρ2)T_{2}\in(\sigma_{2},\rho_{2}). We define T1×T2∈(σ1​σ2,ρ1​ρ2)T_{1}\times T_{2}\in(\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2},\rho_{1}\rho_{2}) as

T1×T2≐T1​ρ1​(T2)=σ1​(T2)​T1T_{1}\times T_{2}\doteq T_{1}\rho_{1}(T_{2})=\sigma_{1}(T_{2})T_{1}

(using the fact that T1∈(σ1,ρ1)T_{1}\in(\sigma_{1},\rho_{1}) for the last equality). The ×\times-product is associative, and distributive with respect to the composition of intertwiners (i.e., their product in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}).

Next we discuss localization properties of the intertwiners. Consider T∈(σ,ρ)T\in(\sigma,\rho), where ρ\rho is supported in 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and σ\sigma in 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}. We call 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} the left support and 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} the right support of the intertwiner TT. If A∈𝒜⁡(𝒪1′)∩𝒜⁡(𝒪2′)A\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime})\cap{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}), then the support and intertwining properties imply

T​A=T​ρ​(A)=σ⁡(A)​T=A​TTA=T\rho(A)=\sigma(A)T=AT

so TT is bilocal, in the sense that T∈(𝒜⁡(𝒪1′)∩𝒜⁡(𝒪2′))′T\in({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime})\cap{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}))^{\prime} (here the commutant is taken in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}). In the case 𝒪1=𝒪2=𝒪\mathcal{O}_{1}=\mathcal{O}_{2}=\mathcal{O}, we have T∈𝒜⁡(𝒪)T\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}) by Haag duality (50) in the vacuum representation and the assumption that π0\pi_{0} is faithful.

We call two intertwiners causally disjoint if their right supports lie space-like to each other and the same holds for their left supports.

Proposition 43.

Let Ti∈(σi,ρi)T_{i}\in(\sigma_{i},\rho_{i}), where ρi,σi∈Δ⁡(𝒪i)\rho_{i},\sigma_{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{O}_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2, with 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} spacelike separated (i.e. T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} are causally disjoint), then

T1×T2=T2×T1.T_{1}\times T_{2}=T_{2}\times T_{1}\,.
Proof.

To see this, note that Ti∈𝒜⁡(𝒪i)T_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}_{i}), so T1×T2=T1​ρ1​(T2)=T1​T2=σ2​(T1)​T2=T2×T1T_{1}\times T_{2}=T_{1}\rho_{1}(T_{2})=T_{1}T_{2}=\sigma_{2}(T_{1})T_{2}=T_{2}\times T_{1}. ∎

The statistics operator ερ\varepsilon_{\rho} is also an intertwiner and it has a nice expression in terms of products of other intertwiners.
