Property (54) generalizes to:

ε⁡(σ1​…,σn,P)​𝑻​(e)=𝑻⁡(P)​ε​(ρ1,…,ρn,P),\varepsilon(\sigma_{1}\dots,\sigma_{n};P)\boldsymbol{T}(e)=\boldsymbol{T}(P)\varepsilon(\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{n};P)\,,

where Ti∈(σi,ρi)T_{i}\in(\sigma_{i},\rho_{i}) i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. If σi=σ\sigma_{i}=\sigma, ρi=ρ\rho_{i}=\rho for all i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, we have

εσ(n)​(P)​𝑻​(e)=𝑻⁡(P)​ερ(n)​(P).\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\sigma}(P)\boldsymbol{T}(e)=\boldsymbol{T}(P)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(P)\,.

To understand better the physical interpretation of ερ(n)​(P)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(P), fix a morphism ρ\rho and consider a family of intertwiners Uk∈(σk,ρ)U_{k}\in(\sigma_{k},\rho), where σk\sigma_{k} are morphisms localized in spacelike separated regions 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}, k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n. Let Ω∈ℋ0\Omega\in\mathcal{H}_{0} be the vacuum vector. Clearly,

⟨π0​(Uk∗)​Ω,π0​(ρ⁡(A))​π0​(Uk∗)​Ω⟩=⟨Ω,π0​(Uk​ρ​(A)​Uk∗)​Ω⟩=⟨Ω,π0​(σk​(A))​Ω⟩=ω0∘σk​(A),\left<\pi_{0}(U_{k}^{*})\Omega,\pi_{0}(\rho(A))\pi_{0}(U_{k}^{*})\Omega\right>=\left<\Omega,\pi_{0}(U_{k}\rho(A)U_{k}^{*})\Omega\right>=\left<\Omega,\pi_{0}(\sigma_{k}(A))\Omega\right>=\omega_{0}\circ\sigma_{k}(A)\,,

so ω0∘σk\omega_{0}\circ\sigma_{k} is a vector state on ρ​𝒜\rho{\mathcal{A}} with the distinguished vector π0​(Uk∗)​Ω\pi_{0}(U_{k}^{*})\Omega.

Now consider vectors of the form

ΨP=π0​(𝑼∗​(P))​Ω,P∈Sn,\Psi_{P}=\pi_{0}(\boldsymbol{U}^{*}(P))\Omega\,,\hskip 20.00003ptP\in S_{n},

which can be interpreted as a product of nn state vectors with identical charge quantum numbers but with an ordering determined by PP. The operator ερ(n)​(Q)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(Q) changes the order of factors in this vector [DHR71]. To see this, recall that Q↦ερ(n)​(Q)∈𝒜Q\mapsto\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(Q)\in{\mathcal{A}} is a unitary representation of SnS_{n}, whereupon ΨP=π0​(ερ(n)​(P)​𝑼∗​(e))​Ω\Psi_{P}=\pi_{0}(\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(P)\boldsymbol{U}^{*}(e))\Omega and

π0​(ερ(n)​(Q))​ΨP=π0​(ερ(n)​(Q)​ερ(n)​(P)​𝑼∗​(e))​Ω=π0​(ερ(n)​(Q​P)​𝑼∗​(e))​Ω=ΨQ​P\pi_{0}(\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(Q))\Psi_{P}=\pi_{0}(\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(Q)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(P)\boldsymbol{U}^{*}(e))\Omega=\pi_{0}(\varepsilon^{(n)}_{\rho}(QP)\boldsymbol{U}^{*}(e))\Omega=\Psi_{QP}

Maybe: Each vector ΨP\Psi_{P} induces the same state on ρn​𝒜\rho^{n}{\mathcal{A}}, namely ω0∘σ1​…​σn\omega_{0}\circ\sigma_{1}\dots\sigma_{n}. Therefore, the action of εQ(n)\varepsilon^{(n)}_{Q} is analogous to permutations of the wave functions of nn identical particles in quantum mechanics, which also leaves expectation values of observable quantities unchanged.

In the next step one introduces the notion of a conjugate sector. Physically, the relation between a sector and its conjugate is that of having a charged particle localized in some compact region versus having the corresponding antiparticle localized in that region. We have already mentioned that sectors can be equipped with the structure of a semigroup and simple sectors form a group. In the latter case, the conjugate sector is just given by the group inverse ερ=±𝟙\varepsilon_{\rho}=\pm\mathds{1}, so we have the simple fermion/boson alternative.

More generally, to obtain a left inverse to a given ρ\rho, we want to find a map ϕ:𝒜→𝒜\phi:{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{A}} with

ϕ⁡(ρ⁡(A)​B​ρ​(C))=A​ϕ​(B)​C,ϕ⁡(A∗​A)≥0,ϕ⁡(𝟙)=𝟙.\phi(\rho(A)B\rho(C))=A\phi(B)C\,,\hskip 10.00002pt\phi(A^{*}A)\geq 0\,,\hskip 10.00002pt\phi(\mathds{1})=\mathds{1}\,.

Note that ϕ\phi on ρ⁡(𝒜)\rho({\mathcal{A}}) can be set as ρ−1\rho^{-1}. We then use the Hahn-Banach theorem to extend the state ω0∘ρ−1\omega_{0}\circ\rho^{-1} on ρ⁡(𝒜)\rho({\mathcal{A}}) to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Let (π¯,ℋ¯,Ω¯)(\overline{\pi},\overline{\mathcal{H}},\overline{\Omega}) be the corresponding GNS triple and define an isometry V:ℋ0→ℋ¯V:\mathcal{H}_{0}\rightarrow\overline{\mathcal{H}}, by means of V​A​Ω=π¯∘ρ⁡(A)​Ω~VA\Omega=\overline{\pi}\circ\rho(A)\tilde{\Omega}. We then define the left inverse of the given sector ρ\rho as ϕ⁡(A)=V∗​π¯​(A)​V\phi(A)=V^{*}\overline{\pi}(A)V.

The left inverse is used to study the representations of the permutation group in d>2d>2 (or the braid group in low dimensions). We note that

ϕ⁡(ερ)​ρ​(A)=ϕ⁡(ερ​ρ2​(A))=ϕ⁡(ρ2​(A)​ερ)=ρ⁡(A)​ϕ​(ερ),\phi(\varepsilon_{\rho})\rho(A)=\phi(\varepsilon_{\rho}\rho^{2}(A))=\phi(\rho^{2}(A)\varepsilon_{\rho})=\rho(A)\phi(\varepsilon_{\rho})\,,

which for irreducible ρ\rho implies

ϕ⁡(ερ)=λρ​𝟙,\phi(\varepsilon_{\rho})=\lambda_{\rho}\mathds{1}\,,

where λρ\lambda_{\rho} is the statistics parameter and it characterizes the statistics of the sector ρ\rho. One finds that the allowable values for this parameter are:

  • •

    λ=1d\lambda=\frac{1}{d}, d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} giving para Bose statistics of order dd;

  • •

    λ=−1d\lambda=-\frac{1}{d}, d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} is giving para Fermion statistics of order dd;

  • •

    λ=0\lambda=0, giving infinite statistics.

In DHR theory, dd is called the statistical dimension.1717 17 Mathematically, as discovered by Longo in [Lon89], dd is in fact the square root of the Jones index of the inclusion ρ⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒪))⊂ρ​(𝒜⁡(𝒪′))′\rho({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}))\subset\rho({\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}))^{\prime}, i.e. it quantifies how badly is the Haag duality broken in the given sector.

To obtain the sector ρ¯\overline{\rho} conjugate to a given sector [ρ][\rho], one shows (under appropriate, physically motivated assumptions, including the finite statistics λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 [DHR71]) that π¯\overline{\pi} satisfies the DHR criterion, so there exists a morphism ρ¯∈Δ⁡(𝒪)\overline{\rho}\in\Delta(\mathcal{O}) such that π¯=π0∘ρ¯\overline{\pi}=\pi_{0}\circ\overline{\rho} and an isometry RR such that ρ¯​ρ​(A)​R=R​A\overline{\rho}\rho(A)R=RA.

In fact, in the language of category theory, localized morphisms and intertwiners form a symmetric (or braided in d<2d<2) monoidal category, where the monoidal structure is given by ×\times. The existence of conjugate sectors (unique up to equivalence) means that the category is rigid.

The reconstruction theorem of Doplicher and Roberts [DR89] allows one to reconstruct the field net ℱ⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}) and the gauge group GG from the above data completing the programme set out in Sec. 8.1. Abstractly, firstly they show the equivalence of the DHR category to a category of representations of some compact group and then reconstruct the group from that category (this step is a version of the Tannaka–Krein duality), together with the algebra of fields on which this group acts.

9 Conclusions

In these notes, we have summarized some important aspects of quantum field theory in the algebraic formulation of Haag and Kastler, focusing on the features that make it very different from quantum mechanics. One such feature is the existence of inequivalent representations. This was illustrated by the case study of the van Hove model in Section 3, and further emphasized in Section 8, where inequivalent representations corresponding to different charges were discussed. In both situations, one can see that all the physical information can be recovered from the abstract net of algebras, so it is more advantageous to think of the net rather than the collection of Hilbert space representations as the fundamental object. The axioms for the net have been formulated in Section 4.1, followed by some simple examples in Section 4.2. The connection between the algebraic and the Hilbert space centred approaches can be made through the choice of an algebraic state. In particular, for QFT on Minkowski spacetime1818 18 Here we focused only on QFT on Minkowski spacetime, but the algebraic approach also easily generalizes to curved spacetimes [BFV03, FV15, FR16]., one can consider the distinguished Poincaré invariant state, the vacuum; we have also described the more general class of quasi-free states that can be specified by their two-point functions and have Fock space representations. In Section 5, we showed that QFT in the vacuum representation has some peculiar features that make it very different from quantum mechanics, the most dramatic being the Reeh-Schlieder theorem.

A net of C∗C^{*}-algebras together with a state induces a net of von Neumann algebras via weak completion. In Section 6 we pointed out that the type of von Neumann algebras that arise in QFT (type III) is very different from the type characteristic for quantum mechanics (type I). We discussed the main consequences of this fact in Section 7, in the context of independence of measurements by spacelike observers, in the guise of the split property.

To close, let us emphasize that AQFT, although very different from quantum mechanics, is not to be regarded as disjoint from “traditional” QFT as presented in standard textbooks. To the contrary, it is a framework that allows one to derive and study common structural and conceptual features of QFT, which then become realized in physical, experimentally testable models.

Appendix A Some basic functional analysis

A general reference for this brief summary is [RS80]. Recall that a Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a complex inner product space, with an inner product ⟨⋅|⋅⟩\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle that is linear in the second slot and conjugate-linear in the first, and for which the associated norm ‖ψ‖:=⟨ψ|ψ⟩\|\psi\|:=\sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle} is complete, i.e., all Cauchy sequences converge. The Hilbert space is separable if it has a finite or countably infinite orthonormal basis, and inseparable otherwise.

A linear operator A:ℋ1→ℋ2A:{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{2} between Hilbert spaces ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} and ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2} is bounded iff ‖A‖≐sup‖x‖1=1‖A​x‖2\|A\|\doteq\sup_{\|x\|_{1}=1}\|Ax\|_{2} is finite, where we use the subscript to denote the Hilbert space norm concerned. For maps between Hilbert spaces, boundedness and continuity are equivalent properties. In this case AA has an adjoint A∗:ℋ2→ℋ1A^{*}:{\mathcal{H}}_{2}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{1}, with the defining property

⟨φ|A​ψ⟩2=⟨A∗​φ|ψ⟩1,\langle\varphi|A\psi\rangle_{2}=\langle A^{*}\varphi|\psi\rangle_{1}\,, (55)

for all ψ∈ℋ1\psi\in{\mathcal{H}}_{1}, φ∈ℋ2\varphi\in{\mathcal{H}}_{2}. Several interesting classes of bounded operator may be defined: a bounded operator A:ℋ→ℋA:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}} is self-adjoint if A=A∗A=A^{*}; while AA is a projection if A=A∗=A2A=A^{*}=A^{2} (more strictly, this defines an ‘orthogonal projection’ but we follow common usage in simply saying ‘projection’). A bounded operator U:ℋ1→ℋ2U:{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{2} is unitary if U∗​U=U​U∗=𝟙U^{*}U=UU^{*}={\mathbb{1}}, and a partial isometry if U∗​UU^{*}U and U​U∗UU^{*} are projections. Every bounded operator A:ℋ→ℋA:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}} has a unique polar decomposition A=U​|A|A=U|A| such that UU is a partial isometry with ker⁡U=ker⁡A\ker U=\ker A, and |A||A| is a positive operator such that |A|2=A∗​A|A|^{2}=A^{*}A. Here, a self-adjoint operator A:ℋ→ℋA:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}} is said to be positive if ⟨ψ|A​ψ⟩≥0\langle\psi|A\psi\rangle\geq 0 for all ψ∈ℋ\psi\in{\mathcal{H}}. For obvious reasons |A||A| is called the positive square root of A∗​AA^{*}A. An operator AA on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is said to be of trace class if ∑α⟨eα||A|​eα⟩\sum_{\alpha}\langle e_{\alpha}|\,|A|e_{\alpha}\rangle is finite, where eαe_{\alpha} is some orthonormal basis of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}; in this case, the trace tr⁡A:=∑α⟨eα|A​eα⟩\tr A:=\sum_{\alpha}\langle e_{\alpha}|Ae_{\alpha}\rangle is finite and independent of the basis used to compute it.

If AA is a partially defined linear map between Hilbert spaces ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} and ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2}, we denote its domain of definition within ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} by D⁡(A)D(A). We typically only consider the situation where D⁡(A)D(A) is dense. If sup{∥Ax∥2:x∈D(A),∥x∥1=1}\sup\{\|Ax\|_{2}:x\in D(A),~\|x\|_{1}=1\} is finite, then AA can be extended by continuity to a unique bounded operator from ℋ1{\mathcal{H}}_{1} to ℋ2{\mathcal{H}}_{2}; otherwise, AA is described as an unbounded operator. The adjoint A∗A^{*} of a densely defined unbounded operator AA is again defined through (55) and D⁡(A∗)D(A^{*}) is the set of all φ∈ℋ\varphi\in\mathcal{H} for which this definition makes sense: φ∈D⁡(A∗)\varphi\in D(A^{*}) if and only if there exists η∈ℋ\eta\in\mathcal{H} such that ⟨φ|A​ψ⟩=⟨η|ψ⟩\langle\varphi|A\psi\rangle=\langle\eta|\psi\rangle holds for all ψ∈D⁡(A)\psi\in D(A), whereupon we write A∗​φ=ηA^{*}\varphi=\eta. An unbounded densely defined operator AA is called self-adjoint if ⟨φ|A​ψ⟩=⟨A​φ|ψ⟩\langle\varphi|A\psi\rangle=\langle A\varphi|\psi\rangle for all φ,ψ∈D⁡(A)\varphi,\psi\in D(A) and in addition D⁡(A∗)=D⁡(A)D(A^{*})=D(A). Any operator is completely described by its graph

Γ⁡(A):={(x,A​x)∈ℋ×ℋ:x∈D⁡(A)}.\Gamma(A):=\{(x,Ax)\in{\mathcal{H}}\times{\mathcal{H}}:x\in D(A)\}.

One says that AA is a closed operator if Γ⁡(A)\Gamma(A) is a closed subset of ℋ×ℋ{\mathcal{H}}\times{\mathcal{H}} with respect to the norm of ℋ⊕ℋ{\mathcal{H}}\oplus{\mathcal{H}}; it is closable if Γ⁡(A)\Gamma(A) has a closure that is the graph of some (closed) operator A¯\overline{A}, which is naturally called the closure of AA. All densely defined operators with densely defined adjoints are closable and their adjoints are closed, so in particular self-adjoint operators are closed. The polar decomposition extends to closed operators.

The spectrum σ⁡(A)\sigma(A) of a (bounded or unbounded) operator AA on a Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is the set of z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} for which A−z​𝟙A-z{\mathbb{1}} fails to have a bounded two-sided inverse. In particular, eigenvalues lie in the spectrum but not every spectral point is an eigenvalue. The spectrum of a self-adjoint operator is real, σ⁡(A)⊂ℝ\sigma(A)\subset\mathbb{R}, while the spectrum of a unitary operator lies on the unit circle in ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Finally, suppose that ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a real Hilbert space (i.e., a real inner product space with a complete induced norm). To distinguish real spaces from complex ones in this appendix, we write the real inner product with round brackets and the adjoint with a dagger. A complex structure on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a linear map J:ℋ→ℋJ:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}} obeying J2=−𝟙J^{2}=-{\mathbb{1}}, J†=−JJ^{\dagger}=-J. Then we may convert ℋ{\mathcal{H}} into a complex Hilbert space by adding two structures: first, the operation of multiplication by a complex scalar,

ℂ×ℋ∋(z,ψ)↦(Re⁡z)​ψ−(Im⁡z)​J​ψ∈ℋ,\mathbb{C}\times{\mathcal{H}}\owns(z,\psi)\mapsto(\Re z)\psi-(\Im z)J\psi\in{\mathcal{H}},

in which sense multiplication by ii is implemented by −J-J (this convention is annoying but avoids a proliferation of minus signs elsewhere in the main body of the text), and second, a sesquilinear inner product

⟨ψ|φ⟩=(ψ,φ)+i⁡(ψ,J​φ).\langle\psi|\varphi\rangle=(\psi,\varphi)+i(\psi,J\varphi).
Exercise 47.

Check that ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, with these additional structures, is indeed a complex Hilbert space.

Appendix B Construction of an algebra from generators and relations

Several algebras encountered in Sec. 4.2 were presented in terms of generators and relations. Here, we give more details on how an algebra may be constructed in this way, taking the real scalar field as our example.

  • •

    First consider the free unital ∗*-algebra 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} containing arbitrary finite linear combinations of finite products of the Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f)’s and Φ​(f)∗\Phi(f)^{*}’s and unit 𝟙{\mathbb{1}}.

  • •

    Construct a two-sided ∗*-ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} in 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} generated by the relations. Thus ℐ\mathcal{I} contains all finite linear combinations of terms of the form

    A⁡(Φ​(f)∗−Φ⁡(f¯))​BA(\Phi(f)^{*}-\Phi(\overline{f}))B

    as AA and BB range over 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and ff ranges over C0∞​(𝕄)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{M}), and similar terms obtained from the other relations, and all terms obtained from these by applying ∗*. Recall that a two-sided ∗*-ideal is a subspace of the algebra that is stable under multiplication by algebra elements on either side, and under the ∗*-operation.

  • •

    The algebra 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) is defined as the quotient 𝒰/ℐ{\mathcal{U}}/{\mathcal{I}}, namely, the vector space quotient, equipped with product and ∗*-operations so that

    [A]​[B]=[A​B],[A]∗=[A∗],𝟙𝒜⁡(𝕄)=[𝟙𝒰].[A][B]=[AB],\hskip 20.00003pt[A]^{*}=[A^{*}],\hskip 20.00003pt{\mathbb{1}}_{{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M})}=[{\mathbb{1}}_{\mathcal{U}}].

    One may check that the fact that ℐ{\mathcal{I}} is a two sided ∗*-ideal guarantees that these operations are well-defined (independent of the choice of representatives).

  • •

    For future reference: let ℬ{\mathcal{B}} be another algebra obtained as a quotient ℬ=𝒱/𝒥{\mathcal{B}}={\mathcal{V}}/{\mathcal{J}}, where 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} is a two-sided ∗*-ideal in a unital ∗*-algebra 𝒱{\mathcal{V}}. Then any function mapping the Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f) into 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} extends uniquely to a unit-preserving ∗*-homomorphism from 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} to 𝒱{\mathcal{V}}, and induces a unit-preserving ∗*-homomorphism from 𝒜⁡(𝕄){\mathcal{A}}(\mathbb{M}) to ℬ{\mathcal{B}}, provided every element of ℐ{\mathcal{I}} is mapped into 𝒥{\mathcal{J}}, i.e., the map on generators is compatible with the relevant relations.

Appendix C Fock space

Let ℋ{\mathcal{H}} be a complex Hilbert space. As usual, ℋ⊙n{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot n} denotes the nn’th symmetric tensor power of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, with ℋ⊙0=ℂ{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot 0}=\mathbb{C}, whereupon the bosonic Fock space over ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is

𝔉⁡(ℋ)=⨁n=0∞ℋ⊙n.{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}})=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot n}.

Thus, a typical Fock space vector is a sequence Ψ=(Ψn)n∈ℕ0\Psi=(\Psi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}}, where Ψn∈ℋ⊙n\Psi_{n}\in{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot n} is called the nn-particle component of Ψ\Psi. In particular the Fock vacuum vector is Ω=(1,0,…)\Omega=(1,0,\ldots), and the number operator NN is defined by

(N​Ψ)n=n​Ψnn∈ℕ0(N\Psi)_{n}=n\Psi_{n}\hskip 20.00003ptn\in\mathbb{N}_{0}

on the domain of all Ψ∈𝔉⁡(ℋ)\Psi\in{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}) for which ∑n=0∞n2​‖Ψn‖2<∞\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n^{2}\|\Psi_{n}\|^{2}<\infty. We will describe the annihilation and creation operators and the number operator on 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}) in the basis-free notation used in Sec. 4.3. See references [BR97, §5.2.1] and [RS75, §X.7] for more details.

In this framework, each ψ∈ℋ\psi\in{\mathcal{H}} labels annihilation and creation operators a⁡(ψ)a(\psi) and a∗​(ψ)a^{*}(\psi) on 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}), with ψ↦a⁡(ψ)\psi\mapsto a(\psi) being antilinear, and ψ↦a∗​(ψ):=a​(ψ)∗\psi\mapsto a^{*}(\psi):=a(\psi)^{*} being linear in ψ\psi. These operators are unbounded and have to be defined on suitable dense domains within 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}), which may be taken as the domain of N1/2N^{1/2}, i.e., those Ψ∈𝔉⁡(ℋ)\Psi\in{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}) for which ∑n=0∞n​‖Ψn‖2<∞\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\|\Psi_{n}\|^{2}<\infty. The annihilation operator acts (on vectors in the domain) by

(a⁡(φ)​Ψ)n=n+1​ℓn+1​(φ)​(Ψn+1)(a(\varphi)\Psi)_{n}=\sqrt{n+1}\ell_{n+1}(\varphi)(\Psi_{n+1})

where ℓn+1​(φ):ℋ⊗(n+1)→ℋ⊗n\ell_{n+1}(\varphi):{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes(n+1)}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes n} is defined by

ℓn+1(φ)(ψ1⊗⋯⊗ψn+1)=⟨φ|ψ1⟩ψ2⊗⋯⊗ψn+1\ell_{n+1}(\varphi)(\psi_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\psi_{n+1})=\langle\varphi|\psi_{1}\rangle\psi_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes\psi_{n+1}

and restricts to a map ℋ⊙(n+1)→ℋ⊙n{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot(n+1)}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{\odot n}. It follows in particular that a⁡(φ)​Ω=0a(\varphi)\Omega=0 for all φ∈ℋ\varphi\in{\mathcal{H}}. One may check that the adjoint operators obey

(a∗​(φ)​Ψ)0=0,(a∗​(φ)​Ψ)n+1=n+1​Sn+1​(φ⊗Ψn),n∈ℕ0(a^{*}(\varphi)\Psi)_{0}=0,\hskip 20.00003pt(a^{*}(\varphi)\Psi)_{n+1}=\sqrt{n+1}S_{n+1}(\varphi\otimes\Psi_{n}),\hskip 20.00003ptn\in\mathbb{N}_{0}

where Sn+1S_{n+1} is the orthogonal projection onto ℋ⊙(n+1){\mathcal{H}}^{\odot(n+1)} in ℋ⊗(n+1){\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes(n+1)}. Acting on vectors Ψ\Psi in the domain of NN, the canonical commutation relations hold in the form

[a⁡(ψ),a∗​(φ)]​Ψ=⟨ψ|φ⟩ℋ​Ψ,[a(\psi),a^{*}(\varphi)]\Psi=\langle\psi|\varphi\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\Psi, (56)

and vectors obtained by acting with sums of products of a∗​(φ)a^{*}(\varphi) operators on Ω\Omega are dense in 𝔉⁡(ℋ){\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}).

This presentation of the annihilation and creation operators may seem unfamiliar to those who prefer their annihilation and creation operators to look more like aia_{i} and aj∗a_{j}^{*}. But let (ei)(e_{i}) be any orthonormal basis for ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and define ai=a⁡(ei)a_{i}=a(e_{i}), ai∗=a​(ei)∗=a∗​(ei)a_{i}^{*}=a(e_{i})^{*}=a^{*}(e_{i}). Then the CCRs become

[ai,aj∗]=⟨ei|ej⟩ℋ​𝟙=δi​j​𝟙[a_{i},a_{j}^{*}]=\langle e_{i}|e_{j}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}{\mathbb{1}}=\delta_{ij}{\mathbb{1}}

(understood as acting on a suitable domain) and of course ai​Ω=a⁡(ei)​Ω=0a_{i}\Omega=a(e_{i})\Omega=0, which provides a set of annihilation and creation operators labelled by a discrete index. At least formally (because infinite sums of unbounded operators should be handled with care)

a⁡(ψ)=∑i⟨ψ|ei⟩​ai,a∗​(φ)=∑i⟨ei|φ⟩​ai∗.a(\psi)=\sum_{i}\langle\psi|e_{i}\rangle a_{i},\hskip 20.00003pta^{*}(\varphi)=\sum_{i}\langle e_{i}|\varphi\rangle a_{i}^{*}.

The advantage of the basis-independent approach is that it does not give any basis a privileged status, and avoids the need for infinite series of the type just given if changing basis, for example. The number operator can also be related to the annihilation and operators in the basis-independent form – see [BR97, §5.2.3].

It is also common in QFT to use annihilation and creation operators indexed by a continuous momentum variables, in situations where ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a space of square-integrable functions of momentum. This is essentially a matter of using a continuuum-normalised ‘improper basis’ for ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, but one should be aware that, while a⁡(𝒌)a({\boldsymbol{k}}) does define an (unbounded) operator, it is sufficiently poorly-behaved that it does not have a densely defined operator adjoint. Nonetheless, any normal-ordered string a∗(𝒌1)⋯a∗(𝒌m)a(𝒌1′)⋯a(𝒌n′)a^{*}({\boldsymbol{k}}_{1})\cdots a^{*}({\boldsymbol{k}}_{m})a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{1})\cdots a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{n}) can be given meaning as a quadratic form, that is, defining its matrix elements as

⟨Ψ|a∗(𝒌1)⋯a∗(𝒌m)a(𝒌1′)⋯a(𝒌n′)Ψ′⟩:=⟨a(𝒌m)⋯a(𝒌1)Ψ|a(𝒌1′)⋯a(𝒌n′)Ψ′⟩\langle\Psi|a^{*}({\boldsymbol{k}}_{1})\cdots a^{*}({\boldsymbol{k}}_{m})a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{1})\cdots a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{n})\Psi^{\prime}\rangle:=\langle a({\boldsymbol{k}}_{m})\cdots a({\boldsymbol{k}}_{1})\Psi|a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{1})\cdots a({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}_{n})\Psi^{\prime}\rangle

on suitable vectors Ψ,Ψ′∈𝔉⁡(ℋ)\Psi,\Psi^{\prime}\in{\mathfrak{F}}({\mathcal{H}}). For more on this viewpoint, see [RS75, §X.7].
